2.2 Hydraulic Cylinder Parameters and Parameter Calculation
2.2.1 Hydraulic Cylinder Parameters and Main Parameters
JB/T10205-2010 stipulates that the basic parameters of hydraulic cylinders should include cylinder bore, piston rod diameter (outer), nominal pressure, stroke, and installation dimensions.
In addition to the basic parameters of hydraulic cylinders stipulated in JB/T10205-2010, there are also standards for nominal pressure thrust and pull force, piston speed, rated pressure, minimum piston rod diameter (outer), plunger diameter for plunger type hydraulic cylinders, extreme or maximum stroke, area ratio of two chambers, threaded oil port and nominal diameter of oil port, piston rod and cylinder outer diameter, piston rod end connection type, piston structure, etc. in other hydraulic cylinder and related standards.
2.2.2 Hydraulic Cylinder Parameter Calculation
The calculation of hydraulic cylinder parameters is mainly for determining the cylinder bore, piston rod diameter, and the selection of seals.
1. Calculation of Cylinder Bore D
The calculation of the cylinder bore D is mainly to determine the thrust or pull force of the hydraulic cylinder, that is, to determine the size of the piston effective area according to the working resistance (load) size and the required working pressure. The calculation formula is:
F=A×p
where: F is the thrust or pull force of the hydraulic cylinder, N;
A is the effective area of the piston, mm²;
p is the working pressure of the hydraulic cylinder, MPa.
In fact, the above formula is only a preliminary estimate. The final determination of the cylinder bore D should also consider the size of the effective cross-sectional area of the piston rod, the strength of the cylinder barrel, the allowable stress of the material, and the sealing structure.
2. Calculation of Piston Rod Diameter d
The calculation of the piston rod diameter d is mainly to determine the strength of the piston rod. The calculation formula is:
d=1.4√(F/(σ×C))
where: d is the piston rod diameter, mm;
F is the pull force borne by the piston rod, N;
σ is the allowable stress of the piston rod material, MPa;
C is the allowable stress coefficient, which is 0.7~0.8.
In fact, the above formula is only a preliminary estimate. The final determination of the piston rod diameter d should also consider the buckling stability of the piston rod, the size of the effective cross-sectional area of the piston rod, the strength of the cylinder barrel, the allowable stress of the material, and the sealing structure.
3. Selection of Seals
The selection of seals should consider the following factors:
1) Working pressure of the hydraulic cylinder.
2) Working temperature of the hydraulic cylinder.
3) Working medium of the hydraulic cylinder.
4) Working speed of the hydraulic cylinder.
5) Working environment of the hydraulic cylinder.
The specific selection of seals should be based on the provisions of the relevant standards and the requirements of the manufacturer.
2.2.3 Hydraulic Cylinder Stroke Calculation
The calculation of the hydraulic cylinder stroke is mainly to determine the maximum stroke of the hydraulic cylinder, that is, to determine the size of the piston travel according to the working requirements. The calculation formula is:
L=S+C
where: L is the maximum stroke of the hydraulic cylinder, mm;
S is the piston travel, mm;
C is the safety margin, generally 50~100mm.
In fact, the above formula is only a preliminary estimate. The final determination of the hydraulic cylinder stroke should also consider the installation size, the strength of the cylinder barrel, the allowable stress of the material, and the sealing structure.
2.2.4 Hydraulic Cylinder Installation Size Calculation

(8) Cylinder efficiency calculation formula
The hydraulic cylinder is a device that converts fluid energy into linear mechanical work, so there is an energy conversion (hydraulic transmission) efficiency problem. The total efficiency ηt of a general hydraulic cylinder consists of the following efficiencies:
1) Mechanical efficiency ηm. Energy loss caused by friction resistance generated by the sealing device of the hydraulic cylinder or the system, generally the mechanical efficiency ηm≥90% of the hydraulic cylinder.
2) Volumetric efficiency ηv. Due to the leakage of the sealing device or system of the hydraulic cylinder, especially when using piston ring sealing, the leakage is greater, generally the volumetric efficiency ηv≥98% of the hydraulic cylinder.
3) Hydraulic pressure efficiency ηy. Due to the hydraulic pressure loss of the hydraulic cylinder, such as the hydraulic pressure acting on the effective area of the cylinder needs to overcome the resistance generated by the back pressure or cushioning pressure.

3. Calculation Example of Piston Rod Diameter

1) For a double-acting single piston rod hydraulic cylinder, if the nominal (or rated) pressure of the hydraulic system, the theoretical output pulling force of the hydraulic cylinder, etc. are given, the piston rod diameter of the hydraulic cylinder can be designed and calculated after selecting the cylinder bore. According to formula (1-2), the following formula can be derived:

$$d = \sqrt{\frac{D^2 - 4F}{\pi p}}$$  \hspace{1cm} (2-22)

where d - piston rod diameter, in mm; D - cylinder bore, in mm; F - theoretical output pulling force of the hydraulic cylinder, in N; p - nominal pressure or rated pressure, in MPa.

If the nominal pressure of the hydraulic system is given as p=16 MPa, the theoretical output pulling force of the hydraulic cylinder is F=200 kN, and the cylinder bore is selected as D=160 mm, then

$$d = \sqrt{\frac{D^2 - 4F}{\pi p}} = \sqrt{\frac{160^2 - 4 \times 200 \times 10^3}{3.1416 \times 16}} \approx 98.41 \text{ mm}$$

According to the regulations of GB/T 23348-2018 and rounding the calculated value, the piston rod diameter of this hydraulic cylinder can be selected as d=90 mm.

Generally, the piston rod diameter cannot be selected as d=100 mm, because under the nominal pressure of the hydraulic system, its output pulling force is only F=π(D^2 - d^2)p/4 = 3.1416(160^2 - 100^2)16/4 N = 196035.21 N = 196.04 kN, which cannot meet the design requirement that the theoretical output pulling force of the hydraulic cylinder should be F=200 kN.

If the nominal force of the hydraulic press is provided by the pulling forces of two or more hydraulic cylinders, when designing and calculating the cylinder bore based on the nominal force of the hydraulic press, attention should still be paid to the conversion of the nominal force.

2) If the ratio of the reciprocating motion speeds or the ratio of the two chamber areas of the hydraulic cylinder is given, the piston rod diameter of the hydraulic cylinder can be designed and calculated after selecting the cylinder bore. According to formula (2-8), the following formula can be derived:

$$d = D\sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{\phi}}$$  \hspace{1cm} (2-23)

or

$$d = D\sqrt{\frac{\phi - 1}{\phi}}$$  \hspace{1cm} (2-24)

where d - piston rod diameter, in mm; D - cylinder bore, in mm; φ - ratio of the cylinder advancing speed to the retracting speed of a double-acting single piston rod hydraulic cylinder; ψ - ratio of the two chamber areas.

Since ψ = 1/φ, when the speed ratio φ is known, the ratio of the two chamber areas ψ can be calculated. Then, according to the regulations of JB/T7939-2010 and rounding the calculated value, the piston rod diameter can be selected according to GB/T 23348-2018; or the piston rod diameter can be directly selected according to the ratio of the two chamber areas.

For example, if the ratio of the two chamber areas is given as ψ=1.46, and the cylinder bore is selected as D=160 mm, then according to formula (2-23),

$$d = D\sqrt{\frac{\psi - 1}{\psi}} = 160\sqrt{\frac{1.46 - 1}{1.46}} \approx 89.81 \text{ mm}$$

According to the regulations of GB/T 23348-2018 and rounding the calculated value, the piston rod diameter of this hydraulic cylinder can be selected as d=90 mm.

3) If the input flow rate of the hydraulic system to the hydraulic cylinder, the retracting speed of the cylinder or the retracting time of the cylinder, etc. are given, the piston rod diameter of the hydraulic cylinder can be designed and calculated after selecting the cylinder bore.

For example, given the retracting speed of the cylinder as v≥70 mm/s, taking the hydraulic system of the WC67Y-100T hydraulic sheet metal bending machine as an example, the input flow rate of this hydraulic system to a single hydraulic cylinder is Q=12.125 L/min. According to formula (2-6), the following formula can be derived:

$$d = \sqrt{D^2 - \frac{Q}{15\pi v \times 10^6}}$$  \hspace{1cm} (2-25)

where d - piston rod diameter, in mm; D - cylinder bore, in mm; Q - input flow rate of the hydraulic system to the rodless chamber of the cylinder, in L/min; v - retracting speed of the cylinder, in mm/s.

For the design and calculation of the piston rod diameter,

$$d = \sqrt{D^2 - \frac{Q}{15\pi v \times 10^6}} = \sqrt{180^2 - \frac{12.125}{15 \times 3.1416 \times 70 \times 10^6}} \approx 169.48 \text{ mm}$$

After rounding the calculated value, the piston rod diameter of this hydraulic cylinder can be selected as d=170 mm (non-standard).

4) If there are no requirements for the speed ratio of the hydraulic cylinder, the piston rod diameter can be preliminarily selected according to the following formula:

$$d = (0.45 \sim 0.7)D$$

According to the main design parameters of the shield propulsion electro-hydraulic system given in reference [76] (see Table 2-17) and the design calculation result of the cylinder bore of the hydraulic cylinder, the piston rod diameter is designed and calculated.

The outer diameter d of the piston rod is selected according to the force situation and working pressure. When the working pressure p>7 MPa, d=0.7D can be taken.

d=0.7D=0.7×200 mm=140 mm

After rounding, the piston rod diameter d can be taken as 160 mm.

2.3 Technical Requirements for Hydraulic Cylinders
2.3.1 Technical Requirements Specified in the Standard for "Hydraulic Cylinders"
(1) General requirements
1) The nominal pressure of the hydraulic cylinder should comply with GB/T 23346.
2) The cylinder diameter and piston rod diameter should comply with GB/T 23348.
3) The thread dimensions of the oil port connection should comply with GB/T 2878.1.
4) The thread type and dimensions of the piston rod should comply with GB 2350.
5) The seal groove should comply with GB/T 2879, GB 2880,
631 Hydraulic Cylinder Manual
148:
Provisions of GB/T 6577—1986 and GB/T 6578.
6) The working environment temperature of the hydraulic cylinder should be within -20~50°C, and the working medium temperature should be within -20~80°C.
(2) Performance requirements
1) The measured value of the minimum starting pressure test should comply with the provisions of Article 6.2.1 in JB/T1020.
2) The measured value of the internal leakage test should comply with the provisions of Article 6.2.2 in JB/T1020.
3) The measured value of the external leakage test should comply with the provisions of Articles 6.2.3.1 and 6.2.3.2 in JB/T1020.
4) The leakage under low pressure should comply with the provisions of Article 6.2.4 in JB/T1020.
5) The pressure resistance should comply with the provisions of Article 6.2.7 in JB/T1020.
6) The cushioning should comply with the provisions of Article 6.2.8 in JB/T1020.
(3) Assembly and appearance requirements
1) The assembly quality of the hydraulic cylinder should comply with the provisions of Article 6.3.2 in JB/T1020.
2) The appearance quality of the hydraulic cylinder should comply with the provisions of Article 6.4 in JB/T1020.
(4) Other requirements
Other requirements stipulated in the contract or technical agreement signed with the customer.
(5) Explanation
When choosing to comply with the "Hydraulic Cylinder" standard, the following explanation should be used in the test report, product catalog, and sales documents:
"The hydraulic cylinder products of our company comply with the provisions of JB/T1020—2010 'Hydraulic Cylinder'."
Note: 1) If possible, the GB 2880 standard should be eliminated from the technical requirements of the hydraulic cylinder, and standards such as GB/T34523—2005, GB/T15242.3—1994, etc. should be added.
2) The working medium temperature is preferably stipulated through the technical agreement as -20~65°C.
3) The factory test is preferably stipulated through the technical agreement to be conducted at room temperature.
4) Green manufacturing and remanufacturing should be appropriately added when drafting and revising the standard to adapt to environmental protection and circular economy requirements.
5) Hydraulic cylinders with special (product) standards are excluded.
6) The aforementioned documents are often used as one of the technical documents provided by the hydraulic cylinder manufacturer to the buyer.
2.3.2 Technical requirements for proportional/servo-controlled hydraulic cylinders
1. Product classification, marking, and basic parameters
(1) Classification
Electro-hydraulic servo valve controlled hydraulic cylinders (hereinafter referred to as servo hydraulic cylinders or hydraulic cylinders) are classified into two types based on the working mode: single-acting servo hydraulic cylinders and double-acting piston-type servo hydraulic cylinders.
(2) Marking
1) Servo hydraulic cylinder model. See the servo hydraulic cylinder model representation method in Section 2.1.2.
2) Servo hydraulic cylinder marking example. See the servo hydraulic cylinder model representation method in Section 2.1.2.
(3) Basic parameters
The basic parameters of the servo hydraulic cylinder should include the cylinder (bore) diameter, piston rod diameter, rated (or nominal) pressure, maximum cylinder stroke, mounting dimensions, etc., and may also include the minimum (temperature) speed, maximum speed, command rated value (such as rated current), sensor parameters, etc.
2. Structure
1) The connecting screws and bolts used for the connection parts of the cylinder body (barrel) in the servo hydraulic cylinder should not be lower than grade 8.8 specified in GB/T30981—2000; the technical requirements for double-ended studs and nuts used for clamping and/or assembly between the cylinder head, cylinder body (barrel), and cylinder bottom are shown in Section 3.17.3 Cylinder assembly double-ended studs and tightening torque.
2) A cushioning device and a gas discharge device may be installed in the servo hydraulic cylinder as required.
3) The servo hydraulic cylinder should have anti-corrosion measures.
4) The strength of the weld seam should not be lower than that of the base material.
5) The sealing elements in the servo hydraulic cylinder should be able to withstand high temperature, corrosion, aging, hydrolysis, and have good sealing performance, with small static and dynamic friction forces, and can meet both the sealing requirements of the hydraulic oil and the application environment.
6) Servo hydraulic cylinders with a mass greater than 15 kg should preferably be equipped with lifting devices for lifting equipment, or the servo hydraulic cylinder should be provided with lifting points, and the set lifting points should be able to withstand a force of 4 times the lifting weight without damage.
3. Requirements
(1) Appearance requirements
The appearance quality of the servo hydraulic cylinder should meet the following requirements:
1) The servo hydraulic cylinder should not have defects such as burrs, bumps, scratches, rust, etc. The coating should not have defects such as pitting, blistering, peeling, or other defects harmful to the surface finish.
2) The surface of castings and forgings should be smooth and free of defects.
3) The weld seam should be flat, uniform, and beautiful, and should not have slag, spatter, etc.
4) For servo hydraulic cylinders with a flange structure, the radial misalignment of the two flange joint surfaces should not be greater than 0.1 mm.
5) External leakage components should undergo anti-rust treatment, or be treated with anti-corrosion treatment such as coating, passivation layer, paint layer, etc.
6) The external surface of the servo hydraulic cylinder should be derusted or have the oxide layer removed before painting, and should not have rust pits; the paint layer should be smooth and uniform, and should not have defects such as pimples.

Generally, the working environmental temperature of the servo hydraulic cylinder should be within -25 to 65°C, and the working medium temperature should be within -20 to 80°C.

(4) Contamination level of working medium

The solid particle contamination level code of the working medium in the servo hydraulic cylinder cavity should not be higher than -/17/14 specified in GB/T14039-2002.

(5) Pressure resistance

The pressure cavity of the servo hydraulic cylinder should be able to withstand 1.5 times its rated (nominal) pressure, maintain pressure for at least 5 minutes, and all cylinder components should not have permanent deformation or damage. The outer surface of the cylinder body (tube) and welds should not have leakage.

(6) Sealing

The servo hydraulic cylinder should have no external leakage at all joint surfaces under 1.25 times the rated (nominal) pressure for at least 5 minutes.

The leakage and low-pressure leakage of the servo hydraulic cylinder should comply with the provisions of 6.2.2, 6.2.3, and 6.2.4 in JB/T10205-2010.

(7) Starting pressure

The starting pressure of the servo hydraulic cylinder should generally be less than or equal to 0.5 MPa. Those with a starting pressure not exceeding 0.3 MPa are low-friction servo hydraulic cylinders.

(8) Friction force during loaded operation

Under simulated actual operating conditions, the maximum friction force during loaded operation of the servo hydraulic cylinder should be less than 2% of its rated load.

(9) Output force efficiency (load efficiency)

The output force efficiency of the servo hydraulic cylinder should not be less than 90%.

(10) Minimum speed

When the cylinder diameter is less than or equal to 200 mm, the minimum speed at which the servo hydraulic cylinder can run smoothly should not exceed 4 mm/s; when the cylinder diameter is greater than 200 mm, the minimum speed at which the servo hydraulic cylinder can run smoothly should not exceed 5 mm/s; or refer to the relevant provisions in Section 3.3.2.

(11) Maximum speed

The maximum speed of the servo hydraulic cylinder is often limited by the piston rod and/or piston seal system and seal ring material. The maximum speed at which the servo hydraulic cylinder can run smoothly can be agreed upon by the manufacturer and user, or refer to the relevant provisions in Section 3.3.2.

(12) Durability

The servo hydraulic cylinder should have a cumulative stroke of not less than 105 m under rated operating conditions.

(13) Frequency response

The frequency response index of the servo hydraulic cylinder (amplitude-frequency bandwidth and phase-frequency bandwidth, or the lower of the two indices) can be agreed upon by the manufacturer and user, or should meet the design requirements.

(14) Step response

The step response index of the servo hydraulic cylinder (step response time) can be agreed upon by the manufacturer and user, or should meet the design requirements.

Connectors should be the same as those of electro-hydraulic servo valves currently in service. It is recommended to select plugs and sockets specified in GJB599A.

The length of the servo hydraulic cylinder includes the length in the fully extended state, neutral position, and fully retracted state.

(2) Structure
1) Under the premise of meeting functional and performance requirements, the structural design of the hydraulic cylinder should be as simple as possible to ensure the safety and reliability of the host machine and minimize maintenance workload.

2) The piping between the electro-hydraulic servo valve and the hydraulic cylinder should be as short as possible and should preferably use rigid pipes; the pipe diameter should be as small as possible while meeting the maximum instantaneous flow rate requirements.

3) Pressure measurement points should comply with the provisions of 7.2 in GB/T28782.2-2012.

4) When sensors, etc. have requirements for preventing relative rotation between the cylinder body and piston rod, the hydraulic cylinder and its installation and connection should be designed (arranged) with structures or mechanisms to prevent relative rotation between the cylinder body and piston rod.

The response frequency of the servo valve should be more than 3 times the highest test frequency of the hydraulic cylinder.

The resonance frequency of the hydraulic cylinder used for dynamic testing of the electro-hydraulic servo valve should be more than 3 times the rated amplitude-frequency bandwidth of the tested electro-hydraulic servo valve.

2.3.4 Safety Technical Requirements for Hydraulic Cylinders
The design and manufacture of hydraulic cylinders must provide basic safety assurance for users' use within the specified service life. Any hydraulic machinery may pose dangers during adjustment, use, and maintenance, so users can only adjust, use, and maintain the hydraulic cylinder according to the safety technical conditions or requirements of that hydraulic machinery to reduce or eliminate dangers.

The following requirements are proposed for hydraulic cylinders, some of which depend on the dangers of the machine in which the hydraulic system is installed. Therefore, the final technical specifications and structure of the required hydraulic system and hydraulic cylinder will depend on the risk assessment and the agreement between the manufacturer and user, but generally should follow:

1) Hydraulic cylinders used in special occasions should undergo risk assessment during design.

2) Measures should be taken to reduce risks during design and manufacture, such as reliable anti-loosening measures for various fasteners.

3) For unavoidable dangers in the design and manufacture of hydraulic cylinders, such as unexpected stroke and accidental falling of the slider driven by the hydraulic cylinder, the host manufacturer should take safety protection measures, including wind (danger) warnings.

4) More specific safety technical requirements (conditions) should be followed according to relevant standards.

1. Applicability
1) Anti-instability. To avoid bending or instability of the piston rod of the hydraulic cylinder at any position, attention should be paid to the stroke length, load, and installation type of the hydraulic cylinder.

2) Structural design. The design of the hydraulic cylinder should consider the predetermined maximum load and pressure peak.

3) Installation rated values. When determining all rated loads of the hydraulic cylinder, its installation type should be considered. Because the rated pressure of the hydraulic cylinder only reflects the pressure-bearing capacity of the cylinder body, it cannot reflect the force transmission capacity of the installation structure.

4) Loads caused by limit positions. When the hydraulic cylinder is used as a limiter, the size of the hydraulic cylinder and its installation type should be determined based on the maximum load caused by the limited component.

5) Impact and vibration resistance. Any components and accessories installed on or connected to the hydraulic cylinder should be installed or connected in a way that prevents loosening due to impact and vibration during use.

6) Accidental pressurization. Measures should be taken in the hydraulic system to prevent accidental pressure increase caused by the effective piston area difference, so that it does not exceed the rated pressure. Attention should also be paid to the fact that due to the area ratio of the hydraulic cylinder and the influence of pressure reduction, the maximum flow rate through the return oil filter of the hydraulic system where the hydraulic cylinder is located may be greater than the maximum flow rate of the pump.

2. Installation and Adjustment
The best installation method for the hydraulic cylinder is to have the reaction force generated by the load act along the centerline of the hydraulic cylinder. The installation of the hydraulic cylinder should minimize (reduce) the following situations:

1) Excessive deformation of the hydraulic cylinder structure due to thrust or tension of the load.

2) Causing lateral or bending loads.

3) The rotation speed of articulated installation types (which may force the adoption of 931 Chapter 2 Design of Hydraulic Cylinders and Their Components

(1) Installation position
The mounting face should not cause deformation of the hydraulic cylinder, and should allow for thermal expansion. The installation position of the hydraulic cylinder should be easily accessible for maintenance, adjustment of cushioning devices, and replacement of complete assemblies.

(2) Fastening hardware
The selection and installation of fastening hardware for the hydraulic cylinder and its accessories should be able to withstand all foreseeable forces. For foot-mounted hydraulic cylinders, the mounting bolts may be subjected to shear forces. If shear loads are involved, consider using hydraulic cylinders with mechanisms designed to withstand shear loads. The fastening hardware used for installation should be sufficient to withstand overturning moments.

3. Cushions and deceleration devices
When internal cushioning is used, the design of the hydraulic cylinder should consider the effects of load deceleration on pressure increases.

4. Adjustable stroke end stops
Measures should be taken to prevent loosening of externally or internally adjustable stroke end stops.

5. Piston stroke
The stroke length (including tolerances) should be specified according to the application of the hydraulic system if not prescribed in the relevant standards.

Tolerances for stroke length are given in JB/T 10205-2010.

6. Piston rod
(1) Materials, surface treatment and protection
Appropriate materials and surface treatments should be selected for the piston rod to minimize wear, corrosion, and foreseeable impact damage.

The piston rod should be protected from foreseeable damage such as indentations, scratches, and corrosion, which can be achieved using protective covers.

(2) Assembly
For assembly, piston rods with threaded ends should have a structure that allows a wrench to apply counterforce, as per ISO 4395. The piston should be reliably fixed to the piston rod.

7. Maintenance of sealing devices and wearing parts
Sealing devices and other wearing parts intended for scheduled maintenance should be easily replaceable.

8. Single-acting piston hydraulic cylinders
Single-acting piston hydraulic cylinders should be designed with a vent port, positioned appropriately to prevent ejected fluid from creating a hazard to personnel.

9. Replacement
Integral hydraulic cylinders should be avoided where possible, but when used, wear-prone parts should be replaceable.

10. Gas venting
(1) Venting position
When installing hydraulic cylinders on stationary industrial machinery, they should be positioned to allow automatic venting or provide an easily accessible external vent port. During installation, the vent port of the hydraulic cylinder should be in the highest position. If these requirements cannot be met, relevant maintenance and usage documentation should be provided.

(2) Vent port
Hydraulic cylinders with a pressurized cavity should be designed or equipped with a vent port to prevent hazards. The hydraulic cylinder should be able to vent air safely through the vent port.

2.4 Design of hydraulic cylinder barrel (tube)
The barrel is the body of the hydraulic cylinder. In a broad sense, the hydraulic cylinder barrel refers to all pressure-bearing components that can form this special sealed pressure vessel, which almost includes all components that make up the hydraulic cylinder. In a narrow sense, the hydraulic cylinder barrel refers to the hollow pressure-bearing part in which the piston and/or piston rod moves reciprocally. The barrel can be closed at one end or open at both ends. The tubular body barrel that is open at both ends is called a cylinder tube.

The barrel is one of the main components of the hydraulic cylinder, and it must be processed using specified materials and meet specific technical requirements.

The barrel referred to in this manual is the narrow sense of the hydraulic cylinder barrel, with a circular inner hole, but not necessarily tubular. Both end faces must be perpendicular to the center (axis) of the inner hole.

Note: 1. It is more appropriate to understand the hydraulic cylinder barrel (tube) as a metal pressure shell. Refer to GB/T 19934.1-2005 for details.

2. In JB/T 12706.1-2016 and JB/T 12706.2-2017, the so-called "square head hydraulic cylinder" has a barrel cross-section that can be either square outer with round inner or cylindrical.

2.4.1 General provisions
The hydraulic cylinder barrel (tube) should have sufficient strength, stiffness, plasticity, and impact toughness. For barrels (tubes) that require later welding of the bottom (end cap), the material (same steel or different steel as the bottom) should have good weldability (such as 35 steel), and the weld strength should not be lower than the strength of the base material. The weld quality should meet the requirements of Class II in GB/T 3323. The raised part of the hydraulic cylinder port (pipe connection) and the bottom (end cap) should be welded synchronously.

For hydraulic cylinders with requirements for wear resistance or corrosion resistance on the barrel bore, a liner structure made of suitable materials can be used inside the bore.

Various barrel (tube) structures are shown in Section 4.9 Hydraulic Cylinder Design and Selection Reference Drawings.

Barrels (tubes) of hydraulic cylinders with the same model produced by the same manufacturer must have interchangeability.

During the design process, the barrel (tube) should be designed with remanufacturing capability, meaning the cylinder tube should have inherent remanufacturing capability.

For hydraulic cylinders used in special occasions, a risk assessment should be conducted on the barrel (tube) during the design phase.

2.4.2 Materials
For hydraulic cylinders or host machines with product standards, the materials should be specified in the product standards or host machine standards.

Cylinder, the cylinder body or cylinder tube should be selected according to the relevant standard requirements, where "cylinder body" generally refers to the hydraulic cylinder body in a broad sense. The mechanical properties ReL (lower yield strength) of the material used to manufacture the cylinder body (tube) should generally not be lower than 280 MPa, and commonly used materials are as follows:

● High-quality carbon structural steel grades: 20, 30, 35, 45, 20Mn, 25Mn, 35Mn.
● Alloy structural steel grades: 20MnVB, 20MnMo, 20MnMoNb, 27SiMn, 30CrMo, 35MnMo, 35Mn2, 42CrMo.
● Low-alloy high-strength structural steel grades: Q355B (C, D).
● Stainless steel grades: 12Cr13, 20Cr13, 06Cr19Ni10 (304), 06Cr17Ni12Mo2 (316), 12Cr18Ni9.
● Cast carbon steel grades: ZG270-500, ZG310-570.
● Gray cast iron grades: HT350.
● Ductile iron grades: QT500-7, QT500-10, QT550-5, QT600-3.
● In special cases, aluminum alloy and other materials may be used.

Reference literature [115] proposes that cast iron can use grades HT200, HT250, HT300, and HT350 or ductile iron. Due to the slightly lower mechanical properties of 20 steel and the inability to be quenched and tempered, it is less commonly used.

When conducting hydraulic cylinder pressure tests, the cylinder body (tube) should be guaranteed not to produce permanent deformation. Under the rated static pressure, any failure mode of the tested pressure cavity as specified in JB/T5924-1991 "Test Methods for Rated Fatigue Pressure and Rated Static Pressure of Pressure Cavities of Hydraulic Components" (already repealed) should not occur.

For the cylinder body (tube) material of hydraulic cylinders operating in an environment with a temperature lower than -50°C, 35 and 45 steel that has been quenched and tempered or low-temperature steel must be selected.

For hydraulic cylinders used in hydraulic presses, some standards stipulate the use of large carbon steel forgings or large alloy steel forgings. For example, JB/T12510-2015 stipulates: The main cylinder and return cylinder are generally manufactured using carbon structural steel forgings as specified in JB/T6397, or can also be manufactured using the method of welding split forgings. The forgings should be quenched and tempered, and appropriate materials and σs values should be selected based on calculated stress, with a safety factor not less than 3. The chemical composition and mechanical properties of the materials should comply with the provisions of the selected material standards, and the inspection items and sampling quantities should comply with the provisions of level V acceptance grouping of forgings in JB/T50000.8-2007, and tangential mechanical properties σs, Rm, A, Z, and K should be tested piece by piece.

JB/T5924-1991 "Test Methods for Rated Fatigue Pressure and Rated Static Pressure of Pressure Cavities of Hydraulic Components" was repealed on May 12, 2017, but so far there is no other standard that stipulates the failure mode of this "pressure cavity" or "pressure shell" of hydraulic cylinders, so it is temporarily expressed as above, and this is also the case in other sections.

In GB/T19934.1-2005 "Fatigue Pressure Test of Metal Pressure Shells in Hydraulic Transmission - Part 1: Test Methods", the failure criteria are stipulated as: ① Any external leakage caused by fatigue; ② Any internal leakage caused by fatigue; ③ Material separation (such as cracks). However, whether it is completely applicable to hydraulic cylinders is a question.

2.4.3 Heat Treatment

Castings and forgings used to manufacture the cylinder body (tube) should adopt heat treatment or other methods to eliminate internal stress. Forgings of forged steel (cast steel), high-quality carbon structural steel, and alloy structural steel used to manufacture the cylinder body (tube) should be quenched and tempered before or after rough machining. 45 steel should be quenched and tempered to 250-280 HBW.

The heat treatment of the cylinder body (tube) can be expressed as: it should be quenched and tempered before or after machining. The cylinder tube that complies with the provisions of JB/T11718-2013 should be given special instructions on the heat treatment state of the delivered cylinder tube by the supplier according to the requirements of the demander at the time of delivery, as agreed upon by both parties.

Reference literature [115] and the previous edition give: Heat treatment: quenching and tempering, hardness 241-285 HBW.

In JB/T8491.1-2008 "Heat Treatment Technical Conditions for Machine Tool Parts - Part 1: Annealing, Normalizing, Quenching and Tempering", the quenching and tempering hardness of 45 steel is stipulated as 200-230 HBW, 220-250 HBW, 250-280 HBW, and 270-300 HBW respectively.

Warning: The cylinder body (tube) must not undergo integral heat treatment with process codes 513 or 513- as specified in GB/T12603 or GB/T16924.

For cylinder tubes that use the cylinder tubes specified in JB/T11718-2013 or other standards with the inner hole surface already finished, and for cylinder bodies (tubes) connected to the cylinder bottom (end cover) by welding, heat treatment cannot be used to eliminate internal stress. Methods such as vibration aging and static pressure stretching can be tried to eliminate internal stress, and the adopted method should be verified for process verification.

(7) Geometric Tolerance

In design, the axis of the inner bore of the cylinder body (tube) is generally determined as the datum element.

1) Circularity of Inner Bore

The circularity of the inner bore of the cylinder body (tube) is divided into four grades, and its tolerance value is expressed as a percentage less than the inner diameter tolerance value. The corresponding relationships are as follows: Grade A—50%; Grade B—60%; Grade C—70%; Grade D—80% (generally not recommended for selection).

Alternatively, the circularity tolerance of the inner bore of the cylinder body (tube) may be required to be no less than Grade 8 (or Grade 7) specified in GB/T 1184-1996, and the circularity tolerance value can be found in Table 2-31.

2) Straightness of Inner Bore Axis

The straightness of the inner bore axis of the cylinder tube is divided into four grades: Grade A—0.06/1000; Grade B—0.20/1000; Grade C—0.50/1000; Grade D—1.00/1000 (generally not recommended for selection). The corresponding values can be found in Table 2-31.

Note: 0.06/1000 means that the straightness tolerance for a length of 1000 mm is 0.06 mm, and so on.

3) Straightness of Surface Element Line of Inner Bore

Alternatively, the straightness tolerance for any 100 mm length of the surface element line of the inner bore of the cylinder may be required to be no less than Grade 7 (or Grade 6) specified in GB/T 1184-1996, and the straightness tolerance value can be found in Table 2-31.

4) Parallelism of Inner Bore Surface Relative to Element Line

The cylindricity error of the inner bore consists of the circularity of the inner bore, the straightness of the inner bore axis, and the parallelism of the inner bore surface relative to the element line. The parallelism tolerance of the inner bore surface element line should be no less than Grade 8 (or Grade 7) specified in GB/T 1184-1996, and the corresponding value can be found in Table 2-31.

5) Cylindricity of Inner Bore

Depending on the functional requirements, the cylindricity tolerance value of the inner bore of the cylinder may be specified separately, especially when the cylindricity tolerance value is required to be less than the combined result of its components. The cylindricity tolerance of the inner bore of the cylinder should be no less than Grade 8 (or Grade 7) specified in GB/T 1184-1996, and the corresponding value can be found in Table 2-31.

6) Perpendicularity of Cylinder Body (Tube) End Face

The two end faces of the cylinder body (tube) should be perpendicular to the axis (centerline) of the inner bore. The perpendicularity tolerance of the flange end face of the cylinder body to the axis of the inner bore should be no less than Grade 7 (or Grade 6) specified in GB/T 1184-1996; the axial circular runout tolerance of the flange end face of the cylinder body should be no less than Grade 8 (or Grade 7) specified in GB/T 1184-1996. The corresponding values can be found in Table 2-31.

7) Perpendicularity and Position of Ear Shaft

When there is a fixed ear shaft on the cylinder body (tube) (at the front end, middle, or rear end), the perpendicularity tolerance of the centerline of the ear shaft to the centerline of the cylinder body should be no less than Grade 9 (or Grade 8) specified in GB/T 1184-1996; the distance between the centerline of the ear shaft and the centerline of the cylinder body should not be greater than 0.03 mm.

8) When the cylinder body (tube) is connected to the cylinder bottom (head) or end cap using threads, a fine-pitch ordinary thread M with Grade 6 precision should be selected.

6) When necessary, the strength and stiffness of the cylinder (tube) should be checked and calculated.

Taking the hydraulic cylinder for hydraulic presses as an example, the cylinder body of a hydraulic cylinder for hydraulic presses is generally a cylindrical part with one end open and one end closed. The structure of the cylinder body generally includes three parts: the bottom, flange, and intermediate thick-walled cylinder (cylinder tube).

The hydraulic cylinder of a hydraulic press bears a large load and operates frequently, and is prone to premature damage due to improper design, manufacturing, or use.

① Stress analysis of the cylinder body. When the hydraulic cylinder is working, high-pressure working medium enters the cylinder body and acts on the piston or piston rod, while the reaction force acts on the bottom of the cylinder and is transmitted to the flange through the cylinder tube (wall). The supporting reaction force on the supporting surface of the crossbeam is used to balance it.

The stress condition of the cylinder body can be analyzed from three aspects: the bottom, flange, and intermediate thick-walled cylinder (cylinder tube).

Both theoretical analysis and stress testing have shown that only in the middle section of the cylinder tube, which is 0.75D1 away from the upper surface of the flange (supporting surface with transitional arc end) and the inner surface of the bottom (with transitional arc), i.e., the so-called intermediate cylinder, can it be calculated for strength as a thick-walled cylinder. The other two sections (parts) cannot be calculated using the general thick-walled cylinder formula due to the influence of the bending moments of the bottom and flange.

The stress analysis of the bottom also has the same problem. If calculated according to the elastic mechanics formula for a circular thin plate with fixed periphery under uniformly distributed load, without considering the actual role and influence of the cylinder wall and the stress concentration in the transitional arc area, the calculated stress may be much lower than the actual stress. Reference [36] proposes a ring-shell coupling solution, which analyzes the bottom, cylinder wall, and flange as a connected whole, and also considers the change in the cross-section of the transitional area. Therefore, the calculated result of the bottom thickness may be closer to the actual value.

If the finite element method is used to analyze and calculate the bottom, the result will be more accurate.

② Strength and deformation calculation of the cylinder tube. For the hydraulic cylinder with front-end round flange or front-end boss installation type, the middle section of the cylinder tube made of low-carbon steel, non-hardened medium-carbon steel, and annealed ductile iron, etc., can be calculated for strength using the von Mises strength criterion according to the theory of elastic mechanics, i.e., the fourth strength theory strength condition. The maximum equivalent stress on the inner wall of the cylinder and the strength condition are:

σmax = √(3R1²R2² - R2²p) ≤ [σ] (2-40)

When the inner diameter D of the cylinder and the allowable stress [σ] of the material are known, the outer diameter D1 of the cylinder tube is derived as:

D1 ≥ D [σ] / ([σ] - √(3p)) (2-41)

Where D—inner diameter of the cylinder, D=2R;

D1—outer diameter of the cylinder tube, D1=2R1;

[σ]—allowable stress of the material, [σ]=σs/ns, where ns is the safety factor, which can be taken as 2～2.5;

p—pressure test pressure of the hydraulic cylinder.

For the hydraulic cylinder with rear-end round flange installation type, the maximum equivalent stress on the inner wall of the cylinder and the strength condition are:

σmax = (3R1⁴ + R4)/(4R1² - R2²)p ≤ [σ] (2-42)

2.5 Design of Hydraulic Cylinder Piston

In GB/T17446-2012, the term piston is defined, that is, a cylinder part that moves in the cylinder bore under the action of fluid pressure and transmits mechanical force and motion.

Usually, the piston is matched with the cylinder bore through sealing components, and divides the cylinder bore into two chambers.

Author's note: The definition of piston given in JB/T41174-2014 is: composed of a piston head and a piston rod, which transmits hydraulic energy during movement, and the piston head is matched with the cylinder bore through sealing to divide the cylinder bore into two chambers. Comparing the above two standards, the problem is not only that the industry standard issued and implemented later is inconsistent with the national standard issued and implemented earlier, but also that the "piston" defined in JB/T41174-2014 itself is not quite reasonable.

2.5.1 Structural Type

The hydraulic cylinder piston should have sufficient strength and guiding length (or sealing length). For pistons that need to be welded to the piston rod, the material should have good weldability.

According to the structural type of the sealing groove on the piston, it is decided whether the piston adopts an integral or combined structure. The sealing system of the piston (combination of sealing, guiding and other components) or gap sealing should be reasonable, reliable, and have a long service life; the connection between the piston and the piston rod must have a reliable connection structure (including locking measures), sufficient connection strength, and be convenient for assembly and disassembly.

The piston has two structures: integral and combined. Pistons using V-rings and other seals are of combined structure. The combined type is also called assembled type in GB2880-1981 "Dimension Series and Tolerances for Narrow-Section Dynamic Sealing Grooves of Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons and Piston Rods".

Various structural types of pistons can be found in Section 4.9 of the Hydraulic Cylinder Design and Selection Reference Drawings.

Pistons of the same model produced by the same manufacturer must have interchangeability.

During the design process, the piston should be given remanufacturability, that is, the piston should have inherent remanufacturability.

Except for the piston and piston rod being of the same integral structure material, other commonly used materials for manufacturing pistons are as follows.

● Carbon structural steel grades: Q235, Q275.

● High-quality carbon structural steel grades: 20, 30, 35, 45.

● Alloy structural steel grade: 40Cr.

● Low-alloy high-strength structural steel grade: Q355B(C,D).

● Gray cast iron grades: HT200, HT225, HT250, HT275, HT300, HT350.

● Nodular cast iron grades: QT400-15, QT400-18, QT450-10.

● Compacted graphite iron grade: RUT300.

2.6 Design of hydraulic cylinder piston rod
GB/T17446-2012 defines the term piston rod, i.e. the cylinder part that is coaxial with and integrated with the piston, transmitting mechanical force and motion from the piston.

In a plunger cylinder, since there is no piston, the hydraulic oil pressure directly acts on the piston rod, so defining the piston rod as the cylinder part that transmits mechanical force and motion is more accurate.

2.6.1 General principles
The hydraulic cylinder piston rod should have sufficient strength, stiffness and impact toughness. For combined (hollow or welded piston and piston rod) piston rods that need to be welded, the material should have good weldability, and the strength of the weld seam should not be lower than the strength index of the base material, and the weld quality should reach Grade II as specified in GB/T3323.

The connection between the piston rod and piston must have a reliable connection structure (including locking measures), sufficient connection strength, and be convenient for disassembly (such as when the piston and piston rod are detachable).

The piston rod and the buffer plunger in the fixed buffer device are preferably made into one piece.

The structural design of the piston rod must be beneficial to improve its bending strength and stability under pressure.

For piston rods with external threads or internal threads at the end, suitable standard wrench flats should be provided. When the piston rod is too small to set the specified flats, they can be omitted.

When welding combined closed hollow piston rods, ventilation holes must be reserved at the outer connection end of the piston rod. For open hollow piston rods, the increase of the hydraulic cylinder internal cavity wet volume should be avoided.

Various structural types of piston rods can be found in Section 4.9 Hydraulic Cylinder Design and Selection Reference Drawings.

Piston rods of the same model of hydraulic cylinders produced by the same manufacturer must have interchangeability.

During the design process, the piston rod should be given remanufacturing properties, i.e. the piston rod should have inherent remanufacturing properties.

2.6.2 Structural types
Piston rods that are coaxial with and integrated with the piston, or piston rods without pistons, can be solid or hollow. However, hollow piston rods should not be made open towards the cylinder bottom side, as that would form too large a rodless cavity wet volume, 841 Hydraulic Cylinder Manual
160:
An excessively large internal cavity volume is generally harmful. Regardless of whether it may affect the inherent frequency of the hydraulic system, hydraulic (spring) stiffness, (step and/or frequency) response characteristics, etc., when the pressurization ends, the elastic potential energy stored in the liquid inside the cylinder may be too large, and when the pressure is released, it may also cause severe vibration of the hydraulic machinery and pipelines.

There may also be a boss at the end of the piston rod in the plunger cylinder, which is used to limit the stroke of the cylinder by abutting against the inner end face of the guide sleeve with this boss shoulder and prevent the piston rod from coming out (shooting out). This boss can also be called the piston rod head, and such a piston rod can also be called a piston rod with a piston rod head.

Some piston rods are designed with a buffer plunger at the end, which is used to slow down the return speed of the piston (rod) at the bottom of the cylinder to prevent the piston from severely impacting the bottom of the cylinder.

The end of the piston rod with external threads for connecting to a flange has a thread on the piston rod that is often designed to only transmit the cylinder return force and cylinder return motion. Therefore, the thread on the piston rod may not comply with the provisions of GB 2350-1980 "Thread Types and Dimension Series for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Systems and Components", and its thread length may be shorter.

2.6.3 Materials

The mechanical properties of the material used to manufacture the piston rod, ReL (lower yield strength), should generally not be lower than 280 MPa. For piston rods with chromium coating, the tensile strength of its body should be greater than or equal to 375 MPa.

The commonly used materials for manufacturing piston rods are as follows.

● High-quality carbon structural steel grades: 35, 45, 50.

● Alloy structural steel grades: 27SiMn, 30CrMo, 30CrMnSiA, 35CrMo, 38CrMoAl, 40Cr, 42CrMo.

● Low-alloy high-strength structural steel grades: Q355B(C, D), Q355E.

● Stainless steel grades: 20Cr13, 06Cr9Ni10 (304), 06Cr17Ni12-Mo2 (316), 12Cr18Ni9, 14Cr17Ni2.

● Cast carbon steel grades: ZG270-500, ZG310-570.

● Others, such as deformed aluminum and aluminum alloys (aluminum alloy forgings), machined bronze, malleable cast iron, chilled cast iron, etc.

Piston rods are generally made of high-quality carbon structural steel 45 or 50, using forging or casting methods; for large-sized piston rods, there are also those made by forging or casting in sections and then welding them with electroslag welding; small piston rods are also made of chilled cast iron.

Now there are piston rods made of alloy structural steel, such as 42CrMo steel, used in hydraulic cylinders for hydraulic presses. For piston rods working under corrosive conditions, stainless steel is mostly used, and stainless steel can also be deposited on the surface of the piston rod.

Special attention should be paid to the detailed requirements of the hydraulic press (machine) for the hydraulic cylinders it uses, such as those stipulated in JB/T12510: "The plunger of the working cylinder is generally made of an integral forging of carbon structural steel specified in JB/T6397, and can also be manufactured by the method of welding split forgings, and should be subjected to corresponding heat treatment. The chemical composition and mechanical properties of the material should comply with the provisions of the selected material standard. The surface of the plunger should be hardened, and the hardness of the working surface should not be lower than 48 HRC, and the thickness of the hardened layer should be greater than 3 mm."

It is not recommended to use materials with higher carbon content, such as 65 steel, as piston rod materials.

2.6.4 Heat Treatment

Piston rods should generally be tempered after rough machining. For piston rods that only bear unidirectional loads, those with low nominal pressure, small cylinder inner diameter, or short stroke, and those with low action frequency, tempering treatment may not be performed. The sliding surface of the piston rod diameter is best to be surface quenched (the piston rod of the static pressure bearing structure should be surface quenched), and after surface quenching, it must be tempered. The process code for surface induction hardening and tempering is 521-04.

Under certain conditions, normalizing or normalizing + tempering can be used instead of tempering.

For welded combined (hollow or welded piston and piston rod) piston rods, heat treatment or other methods to reduce stress should be used to eliminate internal stress.

For piston rods made of 45 steel, their tempering hardness should generally be 250-280 HBW. After surface quenching + tempering of the sliding surface, the hardness should be 45-52 HRC, and it should be relatively uniform. The recommended value of hardness deviation is shown in Table 2-36.

It is advisable to use alloy structural steel. After heat treatment, the surface hardness should not be lower than 52 HRC, and stability treatment should be performed.

The moving surfaces should be plated with hard chromium, and the thickness of the chromium coating (referring to one side after polishing or grinding) should generally be within the range of 0.03 to 0.05 mm; the hardness of the chromium coating should be 800 to 1000 HV; finishing after plating; the coating must be smooth and fine (uniform and dense), and must not have any defects such as peeling, delamination, or blistering; under the maximum design load and/or alternating load, the chromium coating must not have cracks. When the cylinder returns to the end of its stroke, the exposed part of the piston rod should also be plated with hard chromium.

1) The chamfer for installing the sealing element should be determined according to the requirements of the selected sealing element, but it must be rounded at the junction with the outer diameter.

2) The finished piston rod should retain complete center holes.

3) For the piston rod connection type with the risk of accidental sliding block falling in the hydraulic cylinder-driven sliding block, a risk assessment should be conducted during design, and the expected service life should be provided; when the expected service life is reached, the user is required to consciously and timely replace the piston rod.

After the limiting device is invalid, released, or removed, pressure should not be applied to each working chamber of the hydraulic cylinder to prevent various dangers caused by hydraulic cylinder failure.

2.7 Design of Hydraulic Cylinder End Cover

Here, the end cover specifically refers to the rod end end cover (cylinder head) of the hydraulic cylinder, i.e., the front cover of the pressure-bearing shell of the hydraulic cylinder (single rod cylinder) in GB/T 19934.1-2005, but since it is impossible to distinguish between the front and rear end covers of a double rod cylinder, it is more accurate to name it "end cover".

2.7.1 Structural Type

The end cover can be made into an integral structure with the guide sleeve, or it can be made into a separate structure (such as a gland-guide sleeve, end cover-static pressure bearing sleeve), and it can also be divided into a sealed end cover and a non-sealed end cover according to whether there is a seal between the end cover and the cylinder body (barrel), piston rod, and guide sleeve.

The connection between the end cover and the cylinder body (barrel) must have a reliable connection structure (including locking measures) and sufficient connection strength, and at the same time, it should be easy to disassemble and assemble.

The connection between the end cover and the cylinder body (barrel) usually includes flange connection, internal (external) thread connection, internal (external) key connection, tie rod connection, etc. Since the end cover is generally required to be easy to disassemble and assemble, the end cover and the cylinder body (barrel) usually do not use welding connection.

For hydraulic cylinders with high pressure and large inner diameter (such as large hydraulic cylinders specified in the standard), the end cover and the cylinder body should be connected by flanges, and the end face (axial) extrusion sealing type should not be used between the end cover and the cylinder body, including various gaskets given in GB150.3-2011 "Pressure Vessels Part 3: Design". For details, please refer to the relevant content in Reference [108].

The hydraulic cylinder ports on the end cover are divided into axial ports and radial ports according to different opening positions.

The structural types of various end covers are shown in Section 4.9 of the hydraulic cylinder design and selection reference drawings.

End covers with the same structural type produced by the same manufacturer must have interchangeability.

During the design process, the end cover should be given the ability to be remanufactured, i.e., the end cover should have inherent remanufacturability.

2.7.2 Materials
Common materials for integral cylinder heads are described as follows:
● Carbon structural steel grades: Q235, Q275.
● High-quality carbon structural steel grades: 20, 30, 35, 45.
● Alloy structural steel grades: 27SiMn, 30CrMo, 30CrMnSiA, 40Cr, 42CrMo.
● Low-alloy high-strength structural steel grades: Q355B (C, D).
● Stainless steel grades: 12Cr18Ni9, 14Cr17Ni2.
● Cast carbon steel grades: ZG270-500, ZG310-570.
● Gray cast iron grades: HT300, HT350.
● Ductile iron grades: QT400-15, QT400-18, QT450-10, QT500-7, QT500-10, QT550-5, QT600-3.
● Compacted graphite iron grade: RUT500.
● Others, such as bimetallic, die-cast aluminum, cast copper, etc.
For cylinder head guide sleeves or cylinder heads, cast iron may be considered when the nominal pressure p ≤ 10 MPa. Other materials may use high-quality carbon structural steel 20, 35, 45. When welding is required to connect with the cylinder barrel, generally use 20, 35 steel, and stress relief treatment should be performed after welding; for non-welded connections, cylinder heads may use 45 steel and undergo quenching and tempering treatment as appropriate.
The bearing ring is the part that directly contacts the piston rod in steel cylinder heads or guide sleeves.
When conducting hydraulic cylinder pressure tests, the cylinder head should not produce permanent deformation, including crushing. Under rated static pressure, none of the failure modes specified in JB/T5924-1991 "Test Methods for Rated Fatigue Pressure and Rated Static Pressure of Pressure Cavities of Hydraulic Components" (already repealed) should occur in the tested pressure cavity.
Cylinder heads [bearing sleeves (outer sleeves)] of press-fitted static pressure bearing sleeves made from cold-drawn steel bars of high-quality carbon structural steel or alloy structural steel specified in GB/T3078-2008 should have a (cold-drawn) tensile strength not lower than 610 MPa.
The yield strength of materials for cylinder heads of large hydraulic cylinders should not be lower than 280 MPa.
For cylinder head materials with clearance fits between the inner hole and piston rod diameter of H8/f7, H8/h7, H8/f8, H8/f9, H9/f9, and smaller clearances, steel cannot be used.

2.7.3 Heat Treatment
Cylinder heads should generally undergo quenching and tempering treatment after rough machining, especially for forged or cast steel that has not been normalized or annealed. However, tempering must be performed after quenching.
For cylinder heads of hydraulic cylinders with small bore diameters, low nominal pressures, good operating conditions, and low operating frequencies, or for cylinder heads made from non-quenched and tempered steel, heat treatment may not be performed. However, the blank should undergo aging treatment before mechanical processing.

2.8.1 General Principles
The cylinder bottom of a hydraulic cylinder should have sufficient strength, rigidity, and impact toughness. For cylinder bottoms that require subsequent welding to the cylinder body (tube), the material should have good weldability, and the weld seam strength should not be lower than the strength index of the base material. The weld quality should meet the Class II requirements specified in GB/T3323.
The weld seam connecting the cylinder bottom to the cylinder body (tube) should undergo 100% inspection using the method specified in GB/T5777, and the quality should meet the Class I requirements specified in NB/T4701.3.
The connection between the cylinder bottom and the cylinder body (tube) must have a reliable connection structure (including locking measures) and sufficient connection strength.
Cylinder bottoms (bodies) of the same model produced by the same manufacturer must be interchangeable.
2.8.2 Structural Forms
Based on the installation type of the hydraulic cylinder, the cylinder bottom and the rear end fixed single (double) ear ring, circular (square, rectangular) flange, etc., are integrated into one structure.
The cushioning device of the hydraulic cylinder is generally installed on the cylinder bottom, except for the cushioning plunger.
The hydraulic cylinder ports on the cylinder bottom are classified into axial ports and radial ports based on their positions.
Except for the cylinder bottom integrated with the cylinder body (tube), the connection forms between the cylinder bottom and the cylinder body (tube) usually include flange connection, internal (external) thread connection, tie rod connection, welding, etc. Among these, the welding connection between the cylinder bottom and the cylinder body (tube) is the most common connection (fixing) form, i.e., the welding type cylinder bottom using the lock bottom butt welding seam fixing method.
The cylinder body (tube) using the welded cylinder bottom is generally called a sealed cylinder body (tube) or a cylindrical cylinder body (tube).
The inner end face forms of the welded cylinder bottom or forged cylindrical cylinder body (tube) are mostly flat cover types, and there are also concave cylinder bottoms of other types such as elliptical, disc, spherical crown, and hemispherical forms. The cylinder bottom with axial inlet/outlet holes (ports) or liquid charging valve installation holes in the cylinder bottom (center) is called a perforated cylinder bottom.
See Section 4.9 Hydraulic Cylinder Design and Selection Reference Drawings for various structural forms of cylinder bottoms.
2.8.3 Materials
The mechanical properties ReL (lower yield strength) of the materials used to manufacture the cylinder bottom should not be lower than 280 MPa. The commonly used materials are as follows:
● High-quality carbon structural steel grades: 30, 35, 45, 25Mn, 35Mn.
● Alloy structural steel grades: 27SiMn, 30CrMo, 40Cr, 42CrMo.
● Low-alloy high-strength structural steel grades: Q355B(C, D).
● Stainless steel grades: 12Cr18Ni9.
● Cast carbon steel grades: ZG270-500, ZG310-570.
● Nodular cast iron grades: QT400-15, QT400-18, QT450-10, QT500-7, QT500-10, QT550-5, QT600-3.
● Compacted graphite cast iron grades: RUT500.
The material of the welded cylinder bottom should generally be the same type of steel as the cylinder body (tube).
When conducting the hydraulic cylinder pressure test, it should be ensured that the cylinder bottom does not produce permanent deformation, including crushing. Under the rated static pressure, none of the failure modes of the tested pressure cavity specified in JB/T5924-1991 "Test Methods for Rated Fatigue Pressure and Rated Static Pressure of Pressure Cavities of Hydraulic Components" (already obsolete) should occur.
2.8.4 Heat Treatment
Cast and forged parts used to manufacture the cylinder bottom should undergo heat treatment or other methods to reduce stress to eliminate internal stress.
The cylinder bottom should generally undergo quenching and tempering treatment after rough machining, especially for forged steel and cast steel that have not been normalized or annealed, which should undergo heat treatment after rough machining. However, after quenching, high-temperature tempering must be performed, and attention should be paid to the warning in the technical requirements for the hydraulic cylinder body (tube) in this chapter.
For hydraulic cylinder cylinder bottoms with small internal diameters, low nominal pressures, and good working conditions, or cylinder bottoms manufactured using non-quenched and tempered steel, heat treatment may also be omitted.
2.8.5 Geometric Dimensions and Geometric Tolerances
During design, the axis of the buffer hole or the axis of the cooperating stop diameter of the cylinder body (tube) is generally determined as the datum element.
(1) Basic Dimensions
The basic dimensions of the welded cylinder bottom include the cylinder bottom stop diameter, stop height, outer diameter, cylinder bottom thickness, and connection dimensions; for cylinder bottoms with buffer devices designed, such as buffer cavity holes, separate provisions apply.
(2) Stop Diameter
1) The stop diameter is selected based on the inner diameter of the cylinder (body) tube to be installed.
2) The dimensional tolerance of the stop diameter should generally be selected according to js7 specified in GB/T1801-2009; for cylinder bottoms with buffer cavity holes designed, the fit between the cylinder bottom and the cylinder body (tube) can be selected as H7/k6 or H8/k7.
(3) Stop Height
The stop height of the welded cylinder bottom should be sufficient to keep the piston seal at least 20 mm away from the butt weld.
(4) Cylinder Bottom Thickness
The cylinder bottom thickness can generally be selected as 1.2 to 1.3 times the cylinder tube wall thickness; for servo hydraulic cylinder cylinder bottoms, it is recommended to select 1.3 to 1.5 times the cylinder tube wall thickness.

2.8.6 Surface quality
The outer surface of the cylinder bottom should not have visually detectable defects such as shrinkage cavities, inclusions (slag), folds, waves, cracks, scratches, dents, and rust.

Sharp edges on the cylinder bottom, except for the ridge of the sealing groove, should be removed if not shown in the working drawing.

The outer surface of the cylinder bottom should undergo anti-rust treatment, or be protected by a coating or passivation layer, or paint layer. There should be no oxide scale or rust pits on the outer surface before painting. When painting, anti-rust paint should be applied first, then topcoat, and the paint layer should not have defects such as blisters.

2.8.7 Soundness
Forged cylinder bottoms should undergo 100% flaw detection inspection. After non-destructive flaw detection, the cylinder bottom should reach grade I specified in NB/T 47013.3.

Soundness inspection should be performed by eddy current testing according to acceptance grade A specified in GB/T 7735-2004, or by magnetic particle testing according to acceptance grade L4 specified in GB/T 12606.

Under the action of pressure test pressure, there should be no leakage on the outer surface or weld seam of the cylinder bottom.

2.8.8 Strength calculation of cylinder bottom
Strength and stiffness verification calculations should be performed when necessary.

Forged cylindrical cylinder bodies mostly use flat cover-shaped cylinder bottoms rather than concave ones. The center of such cylinder bottoms generally has through holes such as oil inlet/outlet holes or filler valve mounting holes, as well as non-through holes such as buffer cavity holes. Therefore, in force analysis and strength calculation, they are generally regarded as circular thin plates or discs fixed or clamped around the perimeter. Up to now, there is still no relatively simple and authoritative formula for calculating cylinder bottom thickness. The reason is that in addition to the difficulty in determining the working conditions of the hydraulic cylinder bottom, the main problem lies in the mechanical model used to derive the strength calculation formula.

The commonly used formula is the strength calculation formula recommended by Soviet Mikhailov (В.А.Михеев), i.e.

σd=0.75PR2/φδ2≤[σ] (2-50)

where σd - calculated stress, in MPa;
p - hydraulic cylinder pressure test pressure, in MPa;
R - cylinder (inner) radius, in mm;
δ - cylinder bottom thickness, in mm;
φ - coefficient related to the radius Rk of the cylinder bottom oil hole, i.e.
φ=(R-Rk)/R;
[σ] - allowable stress of material, [σ]=σs/ns, safety factor taken as ns≥4~4.5.

In addition, there is the strength calculation formula recommended by Soviet Rozanov (Б.В.Розанов):

σd=PR2/φδ2≤[σ] (2-51)

where φ - coefficient, taken as 0.7~0.8.

The strength calculation formula recommended by German Muller (E.Müller):

σd=0.68PR2/δ2≤[σ] (2-52)

The above three formulas all originate from the elastic mechanics solution for a circular thin plate with fixed perimeter under uniformly distributed load, and the first two formulas consider the influence of holes in the cylinder bottom using φ.

For hydraulic cylinders made of carbon steel and low alloy steel at room temperature, the above formulas can be used for strength calculation.

2.9 Design of Guide Sleeve for Hydraulic Cylinder

The guide sleeve is a sleeve-type cylinder part that guides and supports the piston rod.

2.9.1 Structural Types

The guide sleeve can be made as an integral structure with the cylinder cover, or as a separate structure, i.e., the so-called cylinder cover type and bushing type. Generally, the inner and outer cylindrical surfaces of the guide sleeve are designed and machined with sealing groove slots, used for (equivalent to) piston static sealing, piston rod dynamic sealing, and piston rod dust (sealing).

For steel guide sleeves, the inner hole must also be machined with a support ring installation groove slot, used for guiding and supporting the piston rod.

The guide sleeve must be positioned (with locking measures) and should be easy to disassemble and assemble.

Various structural types of guide sleeves can be found in Section 4.9 of the hydraulic cylinder design and selection reference drawings.

Guide sleeves of the same model from the same manufacturer must have interchangeability.

Note: 1. The guide sleeve with sealing element groove slots is a component of the pressure-bearing shell of the hydraulic cylinder in GB/T19934.1-2005.

2. In GB/T32217-2015, the guide sleeve with support ring installation groove slots is called "support ring groove body".

2.9.2 Materials

The commonly used materials for manufacturing guide sleeves are mainly the following types:

- Gray cast iron grades: HT200, HT250, HT300, HT350.
- Malleable cast iron grades: KTZ650-02, KTZ700-02.
- Ductile iron grades: QTY400-15, QTY400-18, QTY450-10, QTY500-7.
- Compacted graphite iron grades: RuT300, RuT350, RuT400, RuT450.
- Carbon steel, cast carbon steel.
- Others, such as bimetal, (pressure) cast aluminum alloy, cast copper alloy, plastic (non-metallic materials).

In the "Modern Mechanical Design Manual" Volume 2, page 8-14, wear-resistant cast iron grades (HT-1, HT-2, HT-3, QT-1, QT-2, KT-1, KT-2) are given, but except for wear-resistant ductile iron, other relevant standards have not been found.

In JB/T11843-2014 "Wear-resistant Ductile Iron Parts", five grades are specified: QTM1-1, QTM1-2, QTM2-1, QTM2-2, and QTMCD. Among them, L - continuous cooling quenching heat treatment; D - isothermal quenching heat treatment; CD - isothermal quenching heat treatment (resulting in a microstructure of carbides and austenite).

The guide sleeve of the hydraulic cylinder plays a supporting and guiding role when the piston rod reciprocates. The bushing-type guide sleeve can generally be made by casting and machining tin bronze alloys such as ZCuSn6Pb3Zn6, ZCuSn10P1, etc. Some are also made by centrifugal casting of cast nylon 6 with molybdenum disulfide, but due to their poor ability to resist eccentric loads, large thermal expansion, deformation after moisture absorption during processing and assembly, etc., problems such as piston rod swing or eccentricity, jamming of the piston rod, and fracture of the body may occur. Therefore, gray cast iron and ductile iron are currently the most commonly used.

When conducting a pressure test on the hydraulic cylinder, it should be ensured that the guide sleeve does not produce permanent deformation, including crushing. Under the rated static pressure, no failure mode specified in JB/T5924-1991 "Test Method for Rated Fatigue Pressure and Rated Static Pressure of Pressure-Bearing Cavities of Hydraulic Components" (already repealed) should occur.

For the guide sleeve, the fit between the inner hole and the piston rod diameter is H8/f7.
