(4) TPU Coaxial Seal

A coaxial seal with sliding ring made of TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) is becoming increasingly popular, and has been successfully applied in hydraulic cylinders for construction machinery, hydraulic presses, elevators, agricultural machinery, machine tools, molds, booster cylinders, etc. According to a summary by a domestic manufacturer, compared to coaxial seals with sliding ring made of filled PTFE, it has the following characteristics:

1) Better conformity and higher dynamic and static sealing performance.
2) More convenient installation.
3) Better extrusion resistance.
4) The sealing surface of the TPU sealing sliding ring in contact with the inner wall of the cylinder or the outer surface of the piston rod is not sensitive to slight scratches.
5) The processing accuracy requirements for the inner wall of the cylinder or the outer surface of the piston rod can be reduced.
6) Better consistency of material properties for TPU sealing sliding ring.
7) TPU sealing sliding ring has an anti-O-ring extrusion design, which can better protect the elastomer.
8) TPU sealing sliding ring has an oil guide groove structure, which can effectively prevent through leakage.
9) TPU has comparable wear resistance to PTFE material.
10) TPU material coaxial seals have better economy.

Compared to Y-rings or U-rings, TPU coaxial seals have the following characteristics:

1) Lower friction force.
2) Can effectively prevent or reduce the occurrence of crawling and/or abnormal noise in hydraulic cylinders.
3) Comparable pressure holding performance, but better dynamic sealing performance.
4) Better sealing performance at low pressure or low and high speed due to the force applied by the elastomer.
5) Ultra-high hardness TPU material is more pressure and extrusion resistant.
6) No occurrence of back pressure damaging the sealing lip, nor occurrence of burning the sealing lip due to trapped gas.
7) TPU material in polycarbonate system is more heat and working medium resistant than most foreign Y-rings or U-rings materials currently available.
8) Sealing ring with TPU+NBR material combination has lower compression set than single TPU material sealing ring.
9) Sealing groove is compatible with sealing grooves of other domestic and foreign seal manufacturers, making seal selection convenient.
10) Smaller sealing groove, saving space.
11) More convenient installation.
12) Better economy compared to imported sealing rings.

(5) Low Leakage Coaxial Seal
The elastomer of a general coaxial seal is an O-ring, and the friction sealing surface that contacts and seals the mating part is a plastic ring. The elastomer of a low leakage coaxial seal is two O-rings, and the friction sealing surface that contacts and seals the mating part is not only a plastic ring, but also an X-ring, as shown in Figure 2-56.

This type of coaxial seal has better dynamic sealing performance because it adds a rubber seal to the metal and plastic friction sealing surface. At the same time, because it uses two O-rings to press the sliding ring against the mating surface, it has stronger energizing ability for the sliding ring, so its initial sealing (static sealing) performance is better.

In order to prevent the possible oil trapping between the O-ring and the plastic ring from interfering with the energizing (squeezing) of the O-ring on the sliding ring, a pressure relief groove is usually opened on the side of the plastic sliding ring.

The main features of the low-leakage coaxial seal are:
1) Excellent dynamic and static sealing performance.
2) Combining the advantages of combination seals and X seals.
3) High sealing pressure and small leakage.
4) Small structural size, safe and reliable.
5) Low friction, no crawling, long life.

Due to the above characteristics, low-leakage coaxial seals are mainly used in piston accumulators, synchronous control hydraulic cylinders, locking, positioning, support, suspension, servo, digital hydraulic cylinders, etc. With people's understanding and in-depth understanding of them, low-leakage coaxial seals will be applied to various hydraulic cylinders used under medium and heavy load conditions.

(1) Standard Rubber Dust Seal Rings and Their Grooves
Standard rubber dust seal rings refer to rubber dust seal rings (or simply called dust seals) adapted to GB/T6578-2008 "Types, Dimensions, and Tolerances of Dust Seal Ring Grooves for Hydraulic Cylinder Piston Rods" cited in JB/T10205-2010 "Hydraulic Cylinders" and other hydraulic cylinder product standards.
Dust seals are sealing elements that function as wipers (scrapers) to prevent contaminants from entering, or devices installed on reciprocating piston rods (plunger rods) to prevent contaminants from entering. Standard GB/T10708.3-2000 "Dimension Series for Reciprocating Rubber Seals Part 3: Rubber Dust Seal Rings" specifies the types, dimensions, and tolerances of rubber dust seal rings for reciprocating motion.
According to this standard, dust seal rings are classified into three basic types based on their structure and application:

Support rings or guide rings are not defined in GB/T17446-2012 "Vocabulary for Fluid Power Systems and Components." The split annular non-metallic guide element for radial supporting force. In JB/T 8241-1996, the supporting ring is also defined, which is a ring made of wear-resistant plastic material used to prevent collision between the piston and cylinder body, and serves a supporting and guiding function.
Both the piston and piston rod of the hydraulic cylinder must be guided during reciprocating motion. Although the piston's reciprocating motion is nominally guided by the inner diameter of the cylinder barrel, and the piston rod's reciprocating motion is nominally guided by the inner hole of the guide sleeve (or cylinder head), in modern hydraulic cylinders, guide rings (strips) are generally used to contact the cylinder barrel or piston rod. Since the guide ring moves reciprocally on the surface of the coupling part (cylinder barrel or piston rod), it must be wear-resistant. Therefore, it is also called a wear ring (strip).
Regarding the name of the supporting ring, in product catalogs of some domestic and foreign sealing manufacturers, it is rarely called a supporting ring, but more often called a guide ring (strip) or wear ring. There are also those called support rings.
The supporting ring and guide ring are two names for the same sealing element, which has practical significance for hydraulic cylinder seal design. In the composition of the V-ring rubber seal, when the retaining ring and guide ring are made into an integrated structure, it is more accurate to call it a "guide supporting ring." However, since the term "guide supporting ring" has not been defined in the current standard, this manual still uses the term "supporting ring" in its descriptions.
The plastic supporting ring can be considered as a non-metallic bearing to some extent. In the hydraulic cylinder sealing device or system, the supporting ring has the following functions:
1) It serves a supporting function, supporting the piston or piston rod and separating it from the metal surface with relative reciprocating motion.
2) It serves a guiding function, guiding the reciprocating motion of the piston and piston rod and resisting lateral forces.
3) When installed in front of the seal ring, it has the functions of impact resistance and decontamination.
4) It has centering and vibration suppression (absorption) functions.
5) The integral and flanged supporting rings have a certain sealing function.
Common materials currently used for manufacturing supporting rings include: polytetrafluoroethylene + bronze (or with molybdenum disulfide, graphite, etc.), glass fiber reinforced polyoxymethylene, glass fiber reinforced polyamide, fabric (cloth) reinforced polyoxymethylene, fabric (cloth) reinforced polyamide, etc. Their working temperature ranges, except for PTFE mentioned in the standard GB/T 15242.2, which is -40 to 200°C, the other two materials do not have such high usage temperatures, roughly around -40 to 130°C. Please carefully read the product catalogs of sealing manufacturers when selecting specific materials. However, some sealing manufacturers recommend in their product catalogs that the supporting rings used in high-speed light load or potentially crawling conditions can be used at temperatures of -180 to 250°C. Readers who want to adopt this should carefully consider it.
When there is a possibility of crawling, it is more suitable to use a supporting ring made of polytetrafluoroethylene + bronze material; under low-speed heavy load conditions, it is more suitable to use a supporting ring made of fabric reinforced polyoxymethylene or fabric reinforced polyamide (also called fabric reinforced plastic). The tolerance of the S dimension given in the current standard GB/T 15242.4-1994 is not very reasonable, and considerations for material swelling, thermal expansion (such as linear thermal expansion), etc. are not thorough. The S dimension tolerance should be given separately according to the usage temperature range. Although the materials selected for manufacturing guide supporting rings (strips) are all materials with low friction coefficients, if the S dimension tolerance is unreasonable, one situation is poor guidance, and more situations are excessive interference fit. During hydraulic cylinder factory testing, high-temperature tests specified in GB/T15622-2005 are often not performed, which require inputting 90°C working oil into the tested hydraulic cylinder at rated pressure, reciprocating full stroke for 1 hour. Even the test oil temperature rarely reaches 50°C because hydraulic test benches generally cannot heat up the oil and there is no time for it. Therefore, some hydraulic cylinders may experience normal initial operation after field installation, but after running for a period of time, the cylinders may exhibit slower movement speed, crawling (vibration), or abnormal noise. Upon disassembly and inspection, the guide support ring may be severely squeezed or worn. GB/T15242.2-2017 provides four specifications for guide support ring cross-sectional thickness: 1.55mm, 2.5mm, 3mm, and 4mm. However, other specifications such as 2.0mm and 3.5mm are also commonly used. Please refer to the seal manufacturer's product samples when using them.

Plastic guide strips are currently the most commonly used material for making open (cut-type) guide rings. They have a rectangular cross-section with rounded or chamfered edges. Compared to closed (integral-type) guide rings, they have many advantages, especially the ability to be purchased in rolls and cut to any desired length, making installation simple and easy.

Guide strips have basically the same material as the aforementioned guide rings. However, it is easier to treat their surface structure to an ideal condition during the manufacturing process, such as a mesh structure, which improves their lubrication performance, wear resistance, and reduces static and dynamic friction coefficients. This allows hydraulic cylinders to operate at low speeds without crawling.

There are three supply forms of cut-type guide rings on the market: pre-processed tubular material formed into circular rings, spiral shape, and flat rolled guide strips. The cut types generally include three types: diagonal cut (Type A), straight cut (Type B), and lap joint or tongue-and-groove (Type C). Regardless of the cut type, the guide rings must have sufficient cut clearance b2.

The reasons why support rings without sealing function must have sufficient cut clearance b2 or Z (Z1) are:

1) During the operation of the hydraulic cylinder, the temperature will rise. The standard stipulates that the working temperature of the hydraulic cylinder can be ≤80°C. The high-temperature test of the hydraulic cylinder also requires that the hydraulic oil temperature be input into the hydraulic cylinder at 90°C and run back and forth for 1 hour. Because the temperature rises, the plastic support ring will elongate. That is, linear thermal expansion may cause the reciprocating motion part to be stuck (increased friction, rapid oil temperature rise) or even stuck.

2) If the support ring installed in front of the lip seal ring on the piston rod cannot relieve pressure on the "trapped oil," it may squeeze out the support ring (or lip seal ring). Therefore, it is necessary to strive for the support ring to be balanced by the axial force of the hydraulic working medium, while ensuring that the seal ring (mainly the lip seal ring) and its groove are ventilated smoothly.

2) Calculation of support ring width. Assuming the following calculation conditions:
① Radial load F acts uniformly along the support width T (cumulative, not per piece, i.e. the total width of multiple pieces).
② As radial load increases, the contact area between the support ring and the piston (D) or piston rod (d) being supported increases.
③ Radial load F is distributed parabolically along the circumferential contact surface.
④ The maximum clearance of the support ring (radial clearance caused by dimensional tolerances of mating parts and grooves, thickness tolerance of support ring, and pressurization and wear, etc.) is less than the maximum sealing clearance required by the sealing device.

Reference materials provide the following calculation formula:
T=F/n(d(D))p (2-59)
Where T - total support ring width, in mm;
F - radial load, in N;
d(D) - piston rod diameter or piston diameter, in mm;
p - maximum bearing capacity of support ring at operating temperature, in N/mm2;
n - safety factor, generally n≥2.

3) Support and guide design. Support rings play an important role in the hydraulic cylinder sealing system. After preliminary selection, their relative positions to various sealing rings (including spacing, i.e. arrangement), the number of support rings used, and the matching of support rings made of different materials all require further design.

① Support and guide design for piston. For piston sealing systems using bidirectional sealing rings, a support ring should be arranged on each side of the sealing ring. A better arrangement is to add a filled PTFE support ring on each side of the fabric POM, fabric PA, or cotton fiber reinforced phenolic support rings arranged on both sides of the sealing ring. For piston sealing systems using unidirectional sealing rings, a wider support ring should be arranged between the two sealing rings. A better arrangement is to add a filled PTFE support ring on each side of the two sealing rings.

The added filled PTFE support rings have an absorbing (embedding) effect or a dirt-absorbing effect on solid particle contaminants in the hydraulic working medium that may damage the sealing rings and other guide rings, and also increase the guide length. Therefore, these sealing systems are more reasonable, as shown in Figure 2-70. There are more detailed explanations in the piston sealing system of coaxial seals in Table 2-149.

Figure 2-70 Piston sealing system

With reference to the literature, this type of support ring is called a pollution-proof sealing element. Since oil grooves are opened on its sliding surface, it is also said to have the effect of preventing the sealing ring from being "burned" due to adiabatic compression of air.

② Support and guide design for piston rod guide sleeve. For the piston rod sealing system arranged on the guide sleeve (or end cover), when a sealing system composed of coaxial seals + lip sealing ring + dust-proof sealing ring is used, support rings should generally be arranged on both sides of the coaxial seals. A better arrangement is to arrange a filled PTFE support ring or a filled PTFE support ring + coaxial seal + fabric POM, fabric PA, or cotton fiber reinforced phenolic support ring + lip sealing ring + fabric POM, fabric PA, or cotton fiber reinforced phenolic + dust-proof sealing ring in front of the fabric POM, fabric PA, or cotton fiber reinforced phenolic support ring arranged in front of the coaxial seal.

The filled PTFE support ring is arranged in front of the fabric POM, fabric PA, or cotton fiber reinforced phenolic support ring (on the side of the hydraulic cylinder working medium action), and its function is the same as above. The piston rod sealing system with only one filled PTFE support ring (three support rings in total) arranged in front of the coaxial seal has a longer supporting length for the moving parts of the hydraulic cylinder (including the piston and piston rod), so it is more reasonable, as shown in Figure 2-71. More detailed technical parameters can be found in Table 2-150 coaxial seal + lip sealing ring piston rod sealing system.

Figure 2-71 Piston rod sealing system

4) Groove design.

① Design principles for support ring installation grooves:

a. The radial depth of the groove should be as shallow as possible. Only in this way can the piston or piston rod be separated from the metal surface with relative reciprocating motion as much as possible to avoid collision. A thicker support ring should be used if necessary.

b. A wider support ring should be used as much as possible within the allowable length (width) of the piston or guide sleeve (cylinder head).

c. The tolerance level of the bottom dimension of the groove should be one level higher than that of the sealing groove bottom dimension of other sealing rings (excluding dust-proof rings) in the sealing system.

d. The side of the groove should be perpendicular to the bottom of the groove, and the fillet at the bottom of the groove should not be larger than the specified value to prevent it from "holding" here, causing the edge of the support ring to be tightly fitted or stuck with the mating part.

e. For multiple support rings, the bottom surfaces of their grooves must be coaxial, and one of the groove bottom surfaces can be used as the coaxiality reference for the groove bottom surfaces of other sealing elements.

f. The spacing between two adjacent support rings should be greater than the depth of their groove; the spacing with other sealing elements should be greater than the depth of the groove of this sealing element.

② Precautions for support ring installation groove design:

a. Both POM and PA materials have the problem of water absorption and expansion. During processing, storage, assembly, and use, serious problems may be caused by water absorption (or dimensional changes) due to water washing, moisture in the air, moisture absorption, etc., and mainly due to excessive water content in the hydraulic oil. The problem that occurs is that the relative reciprocating moving part is tightly fitted (expanded) or stuck (expanded to death).

b. The thickness tolerance of the support ring may be one of the main problems of domestic guide rings, and products from the same manufacturer in different batches may be different each time.

c. The length dimension and tolerance of the groove should also be designed and manufactured according to the standards or product samples.

d. The depth of the groove should not be less than the specified minimum depth.

13. Retaining ring and its groove

(1) Retaining ring and groove for O-ring

The O-ring is equipped with a retaining ring to increase the working pressure and service life of the O-ring and prevent the O-ring from being squeezed into the low-pressure side gap; when the pressure is further increased, the O-ring is squeezed out from the mating gap.
287:
Damage. The installation of a retaining ring greatly increases the sealing pressure of the O-ring seal, with static sealing up to 63 MPa and dynamic sealing up to 35 MPa. When the working pressure of the dynamic seal exceeds 10 MPa (or when the static seal exceeds 16 MPa), consideration should be given to installing a retaining ring. The number of retaining rings to be installed is determined based on the pressure condition of the O-ring: one retaining ring for unidirectional pressure, installed on the side where the O-ring may be extruded; two retaining rings for bidirectional pressure, with the O-ring sandwiched between the two retaining rings. The author once used a single O-ring seal at the bottom of the two sets of 8 hydraulic cylinder barrels in a hydraulic tilter, and the seal almost completely failed during testing. After modifying the seal groove at the bottom of the cylinder and installing retaining rings, this problem was solved. The most commonly used material for processing retaining rings is polytetrafluoroethylene, but nylon 6 or nylon 1010 can also be used. It is generally believed that when the O-ring retaining ring is in contact with the mating part, installing a retaining ring for dynamic sealing may increase the friction force, and even on hydraulic cylinders of hydraulic presses, it may cause problems such as the slider being unable to move down quickly.

Here, it is emphasized once again that whether an O-ring needs to be equipped with a retaining ring, in addition to considering the working pressure or nominal pressure (rated pressure) of the hydraulic cylinder, factors such as the mating clearance or single-sided (maximum) clearance (extrusion clearance) should also be considered.

There is currently no standard for the size series and tolerances of O-ring retaining rings. Foreign products can be purchased as a set, while domestic hydraulic cylinder manufacturers generally design and manufacture them themselves.

Note: GB/T 3452.4-XXXX "Rubber O-rings for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Applications Part 4: Anti-extrusion Rings (Retaining Rings)" is being developed, but the author has put forward some opinions on the submitted draft, including disagreement with determining the outer diameter size and tolerance of the O-ring retaining ring for pistons based on the piston diameter plus tolerance.

As shown in Figure 2-72, the cross-sectional shape of the O-ring retaining ring is usually rectangular; there are three types: integral, bevel-cut, and spiral. There is also a type of O-ring retaining ring as shown in Figure 2-72 d, which is called a concave retaining ring because it is concave with the O-ring extrusion surface, which can more favorably protect the O-ring.

The design of the retaining ring should follow the following principles: distinguish between shaft type and hole type, the tolerance of the inner diameter of the shaft type (sealing) retaining ring should be small, and the tolerance of the outer diameter of the hole type (sealing) retaining ring should be small; after the installation of the retaining ring occupies the width of the seal groove, the remaining groove width (cavity) should still meet the expansion requirements of the O-ring. According to the analysis of GB/T 3452.3-2005 "O-ring Grooves for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Applications", the thickness of the retaining ring with a cross-section of 1.80 mm, 2.65 mm, and 3.55 mm should be 1.4 mm, the thickness of the retaining ring with a cross-section of 5.30 mm should be 1.9 mm, and the thickness of the retaining ring with a cross-section of 7.00 mm should be 2.8 mm. Considering the tolerance of the seal groove width and the plastic material of the retaining ring, the thickness of the retaining ring can generally be determined as: 1.5 mm, 2.0 mm, 3.0 mm; there must be a clearance between the retaining ring and the moving mating surface, and the mating part must not be clamped (or expanded) or clamped (or expanded) to death, otherwise the friction force may increase greatly.

Figure 2-72 Type of O-ring retaining ring

a) Integral type b) Bevel-cut type c) Spiral type d) Concave type

When the working pressure is ≤31.5 MPa, it is advisable to select the size and tolerance of the O-ring retaining ring according to Table 2-135. Now, in various documents and materials, the descriptions of O-ring retaining rings vary, and readers should be cautious when designing and using them.

Table 2-135 gives the size and tolerance of the retaining ring. When using it, select according to the nominal diameter (d or D), nominal (or rated) pressure, mating clearance, working temperature, working time, static or dynamic sealing, retaining ring material, etc.

Special emphasis is placed on:

1) When using polyamide plastics PA06, PA1010 (nylon 06, nylon 1010) and other materials to make retaining rings, the size of the retaining ring may change due to water or moisture (humidity), so it is required to prevent the retaining ring from coming into contact with water and moisture during processing, storage, assembly and use, and even the water content of the hydraulic oil should be strictly controlled.

2) As shown in Figure 2-73, the O-ring extrusion surface (contact surface) must not be chamfered (rounded), while the chamfer or rounding must be provided at the contact with the bottom corner of the groove. The chamfer or rounding size is shown in Table 2-136.

3) When cutting the retaining ring at an angle of 22° to 30°, the cut should be 0 to 0.15 mm, but it is absolutely not allowed to have "missing meat" on the O-ring extrusion surface or extrusion surface.

(2) Retaining ring for U-ring and its groove

In some seal product samples, the retaining ring for U-ring is also called a support ring. In order to distinguish it from the support ring that has been defined by the standard, it is uniformly referred to as the retaining ring for U-ring (or simply as a retaining ring) in the following description.

Principles for Selecting Retaining Ring Materials for U-rings:
1) The maximum extrusion gap appears when the maximum eccentricity occurs, and the ultimate extrusion resistance of the retaining ring material must meet the requirements of the maximum extrusion gap.
2) The ultimate extrusion resistance of a certain type of retaining ring material is closely related to the maximum working pressure, maximum working temperature, working time, etc.
3) In Table 2-138, the extrusion resistance of materials increases from top to bottom, among which 10FF, 34WF, and 31BF retaining ring materials are mainly used for U-rings made of NBR or FKM rubber materials.
The ultimate extrusion resistance of a certain type of retaining ring material is expressed as the ultimate extrusion gap, which is obtained through theoretical calculation and experimental verification under certain conditions.
When the maximum extrusion gap exceeds the ultimate extrusion gap, U-rings with retaining rings also do not have a long service life. As the working pressure, working temperature, and working time increase, the maximum extrusion resistance of the retaining ring decreases, and the service life is also shortened.
Generally, the maximum eccentricity (allowable eccentricity) of the U-ring should be less than 20% of the pre-compression of the U-ring in the U-ring sealing groove; the maximum extrusion gap is the sum of the maximum unilateral fit clearance and the maximum eccentricity.

15. High Temperature and High Pressure Sealing Ring
The hydraulic cylinder is an energy conversion device, and a part of energy will inevitably be lost, and most of this lost energy is converted into thermal energy. The (ultra) high-pressure hydraulic cylinder can convert higher (more) energy under the same volume and weight, so current hydraulic systems and components are pursuing high pressure or ultra-high pressure. High pressure is often accompanied by high temperature in many cases. In order to reduce the highest working temperature of hydraulic systems and components, a cooling system is generally required, but this also requires energy.

If hydraulic systems and components are allowed to operate at certain high temperatures and high pressures, at least the energy for the cooling system can be saved. As an actuator, the hydraulic cylinder not only generates heat by itself, but may also cause the temperature to be higher than the system temperature due to the transfer of thermal energy by the driven load and thermal radiation from the surrounding environment. Therefore, the sealing design of the hydraulic cylinder must predict the working temperature range.

Now, the design of the sealing system for hydraulic cylinders with a highest working temperature of 150°C and a highest working pressure ≤35 MPa has become increasingly mature, but the design of the sealing system for hydraulic cylinders under higher temperatures and pressures must be cautious.

The non-typical U-shaped ring (with embedded metal spring) piston sealing system introduced in Table 2-149 may have a working temperature range of -60 to 150°C.

(1) Maximum working temperature of sealing material
In HG/T 25792008 "O-ring Rubber Seals for General Hydraulic Systems", O-ring rubber sealing materials with working temperature ranges of -40~100°C and -25~125°C are specified.
In HG/T 20212014 "High Temperature Grease O-ring Rubber Seals", the sealing materials are classified into Class I, II, III and IV according to different media. Class I is represented by nitrile rubber NBR, suitable for petroleum-based grease, with a general working temperature range of -25~125°C, and can reach 150°C for short periods. Class II is represented by low compression set fluoroelastomer FKM, suitable for synthetic ester lubricants, with a general working temperature range of -15~200°C, and can reach 250°C for short periods. Class III is represented by acrylate rubber ACM and ethylene acrylate rubber AEM, suitable for petroleum-based lubricants, with a general working temperature range of -20~150°C, and can reach 175°C for short periods. Class IV is represented by hydrogenated nitrile rubber HNBR, suitable for petroleum-based lubricants, with a general working temperature range of -25~150°C, and can reach 160°C for short periods.

In HG/T28102008 "Rubber Seal Materials for Reciprocating Motion", the sealing materials are classified into Class A and B. Class A is nitrile rubber material, with a working temperature range of -30~100°C. Class B is castable polyurethane material, with a working temperature range of -40~80°C.

(2) Maximum working temperature of seal ring
According to the high temperature test specified in JB/T102052010 "Hydraulic Cylinder": Under rated pressure, 90°C working oil is input into the tested hydraulic cylinder, and full-stroke reciprocating operation for 1h should meet the high temperature performance requirements agreed upon by the customer and manufacturer. At the same time, it is stipulated that under normal circumstances, the working environment temperature of the hydraulic cylinder should be within the range of -20~50°C, and the working medium temperature should be within the range of -20~80°C. In GB/T79352005 "General Technical Conditions for Hydraulic Components", it is stipulated that except for special provisions, the oil temperature during testing should be 50°C (Class A ±1.0°C, Class B ±2.0°C, Class C ±4.0°C). In GB/T156222005 "Test Method for Hydraulic Cylinder", it is stipulated that except for special provisions, type tests should be conducted at 50°C±2°C, and factory tests should be conducted at 50°C±4°C.

In GB/T34521-2005 "O-ring Rubber Seals for Hydraulic and Pneumatic Use Part 1: Size Series and Tolerances", no provisions are made for working temperature.

In JB/T10752006 "O-ring Rubber Seals for Mechanical Seals", the working temperature range of nitrile rubber O-ring is specified as -30~100°C, and the working temperature range of fluoroelastomer is specified as -20~200°C.

In JB/T107062007 "Fluoroplastic Coated Rubber O-ring for Mechanical Seals", the working temperature range is specified as -60~200°C (FEP coated fluoroelastomer is -20~180°C, silicone rubber coated FEP is -60~180°C, fluoroelastomer coated PFA is -20~200°C, silicone rubber coated is -60~200°C).

In GB/T152421-2017 "Size Series of Dynamic Sealing Devices for Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons and Piston Rods Part 1: Size Series and Tolerances of Coaxial Seals", no provisions are made for working temperature.

In GB/T152422-2017 "Size Series of Dynamic Sealing Devices for Hydraulic Cylinder Pistons and Piston Rods Part 2: Size Series and Tolerances of Support Rings", the working temperature range is specified as -30~100°C (polyethylene).

2.10.6 Common Hydraulic Cylinder Sealing Structure Types

1. Definition of Hydraulic Cylinder Sealing System

In hydraulic cylinder sealing and design, professional terms or vocabulary such as sealing components (rings), combined sealing components (rings), composite sealing rings, and sealing devices are often used. Nowadays, the term "hydraulic cylinder sealing system" is frequently used in domestic and foreign sealing component product samples, including in standards. However, this term has not been defined in any domestic standard so far.

The author attempts to give the following definition of the term "hydraulic cylinder sealing system", which is a configuration of sealing components arranged in series according to the requirements of hydraulic cylinder sealing to generate sealing, control leakage, and/or prevent pollution.

It should be noted that the sealing components here specifically refer to the general term for sealing rings, retaining rings, support rings (guide rings), and dust seals used on hydraulic cylinders. That is, the sealing device is a device composed of one or more sealing components and supporting parts (such as retaining rings, springs, metal shells), plus guide rings, support rings, and support rings.

The term "hydraulic cylinder sealing system" has its definite connotation and extension. Its connotation is:

1) It must be a configuration of two or more sealing components. A single sealing component cannot be called a sealing system.

2) Two or more sealing components used to seal the same leakage gap (or mating gap) can only be arranged in series (configured).

3) The sealing system must be able to generate sealing, control leakage, and/or prevent pollution.

4) The sealing system must be able to meet the requirements of hydraulic cylinder sealing under specific working conditions.

For back-to-back piston seals, strictly speaking, they cannot be called a sealing system. However, for convenience of expression, this manual sometimes also classifies the seal configurations described in 1) and 2) above as part of the piston seal system.

3) A hydraulic cylinder sealing system generally consists of two sub-sealing systems: the piston sealing system and the piston rod sealing system.

4) The hydraulic cylinder sealing system must meet the sealing (performance) requirements of the hydraulic cylinder.

5) The emphasis of the hydraulic cylinder sealing system (feature) is the coordination and unified configuration among various sealing elements.

Its extension is: applicable to cylinder seals.

To express the sealing system in hydraulic cylinder sealing and its design, the following representation methods are established:

1) The piston sealing system is described starting from the oil port of the rodless chamber of the hydraulic cylinder, and the piston rod sealing system is described starting from the nearest seal to the oil port of the hydraulic cylinder (rod chamber).

2) For double-rod cylinders, the piston sealing system is described starting from the seal nearest to the oil port on the left side of the drawing.

3) Sealing elements with defined (symbol) are represented according to the definition; those without defined (symbol) are expressed in Chinese, and series configuration is indicated by the "+" sign.

4) Sealing elements assembled on the same component are generally described in one sealing system.

5) The applicable conditions for the sealing system are tentatively set as: maximum working pressure or pressure range, maximum working temperature or temperature range, and maximum reciprocating motion speed or speed range.

The applicable conditions for the sealing system can be further referenced in Table 2-157 "Summary of Rated Conditions for Hydraulic Cylinder Sealing Design."

6) The hydraulic working medium for hydraulic cylinders is generally hydraulic oil or other mineral oils with equivalent performance. If other working media are used, such as water-ethylene glycol, phosphate ester fire-resistant hydraulic fluids, etc., they need to be specifically noted.

2. 1 0 . 7 Several Specific Issues in Hydraulic Cylinder Seal System Design
1. Groove spacing problem
Determining the minimum distance between (seal) grooves is a common problem encountered in hydraulic cylinder seal system design. Reasonable design of groove spacing can achieve the optimal structural dimensions of the hydraulic cylinder while ensuring reliable sealing, thereby achieving optimized design of the hydraulic cylinder seal system structure. Hydraulic cylinder seal system design not only includes the arrangement (configuration) of each sealing element, but also the determination of spacing between sealing elements. Only by ensuring the dimensional and shape stability of each (seal) groove can the sealing performance of the piston seal system or piston rod seal system be guaranteed.
The side wall of the groove on the part body is generally called the edge wall. If the strength and rigidity of the edge wall are insufficient, the groove side may bend, or even the edge wall may be sheared, leading to seal failure.
In the design of hydraulic cylinder piston rod seal system, for the spacing between seal grooves (including dust seal ring) of two coaxial sealing elements in the piston rod seal system, if only considering strength and rigidity, it should generally not be less than the depth of the deepest groove among them, as shown in Figure 2 - 7 8.
The spacing between buffer seal ring and other sealing elements should be greater.
In the design of hydraulic cylinder piston seal system, due to the action of alternating pressure, if the groove spacing between sealing elements is only considered from the perspective of strength and rigidity, it should be at least greater than 1 . 5 times the depth of the deepest groove among them.
The spacing between support ring and other sealing elements is generally 1 . 5 to 2 times the depth of the support ring installation groove.
Under special circumstances, necessary strength calculations should be performed on the edge wall.

3. Opening of leakage channels
As shown in Figure 2-79, if possible, it is best to open a leakage channel in front of the dust seal.

Figure 2-79 Opening of leakage channel in front of dust seal

This is because:
1) A single-lip rubber dust seal only has a dust-proof function, and does not have an auxiliary sealing function.
2) Even when using a double-lip rubber dust seal, it is very difficult to achieve "zero" leakage.
3) Even if the external leakage of the hydraulic cylinder is "zero" under a certain specific working condition, once the working condition changes (such as an increase in oil temperature), external leakage may occur, only the amount of leakage varies.

Precisely because of this, only by channeling the "leaking oil" in front of the dust seal through a leakage channel directly into an open oil tank or other open container can the dust seal always seal the hydraulic oil at "zero" pressure, and its sealing performance can be maintained for a relatively long time. The external leakage at the piston rod can be guaranteed to be minimal or "zero" under changing working conditions.

If a leakage channel is opened in front of the dust seal, the dust seal used should be a double-lip nitrile rubber seal.

It should be noted here: ① In the schematic diagram of the test device specified in GB/T32217—2016, the setting position of the "leakage measurement port" has important reference value for the setting of other hydraulic cylinder leakage channels, and its specified "leakage collection area" (for a piston rod diameter of Φ36 mm and a length of (20 mm ± 5 mm)) is also very important. ② Some products now open the leakage channel in front of the second seal ring of the piston rod seal system, which is incorrect.

4. Selection of single and double lip dust seals
The dust seal is an important component of the piston rod seal system and should receive due attention.

GB/T10708.3—2000 "Rubber Seals for Reciprocating Motion - Part 3: Rubber Dust Seals" stipulates three basic types of dust seals, two of which are single-lip dust seals and one is a double-lip dust seal.

In the piston rod seal system, whether a single-lip or double-lip dust seal is used, it is very difficult to achieve "zero" leakage at the piston rod, only that the single-lip dust seal may be leaking continuously; while the double-lip dust seal may occasionally experience a large amount of leakage once.

In the piston rod seal system with coaxial sealing elements (the coaxial sealing element is close to the dust seal), regardless of whether this coaxial sealing element has a "rod return" function, a double-lip dust seal should be used.

In the piston rod seal system with lip seals (the lip seal is close to the dust seal), a single-lip dust seal should generally be used.

Single-lip dust seals and double-lip dust seals are also often referred to as single-acting dust seals and double-acting dust seals. During the return stroke of the cylinder (rod retraction), the dust seal has the function of scraping contaminants on the piston rod, such as mud, dust, and condensed water; the other function of the double-acting dust seal is to scrape off the oil film that leaks after being sealed by other sealing elements, further optimizing the sealing performance of the sealing system. However, regardless of whether it is a single-acting or double-acting dust seal, taking the dust seal specified in GB/T10708.3—2000 as an example, if the pressure it bears is too high, it may be squeezed out of the groove.

Dust seals generally do not have specified applicable pressures or rated pressures. Even double-lip dust seals mainly scrape oil rather than seal, or have an auxiliary sealing function.

Commonly used nitrile rubber dust seals and polyurethane rubber dust seals require lubrication. Because the sliding ring material of the sliding ring dust seal may be filled with polytetrafluoroethylene, the requirements for lubrication are not very strict. Dust seals lacking lubrication have a shorter service life, especially polyurethane dust seals, which may also produce abnormal noise during the reciprocating motion of the piston rod.

There are special structural (including material) designs for dust seals to prevent them from being squeezed out and to prevent them from scraping ice.

2.1.0.8 Preliminary determination of sealing conditions for hydraulic cylinders
The sealing conditions of a hydraulic cylinder are a set of characteristic values that the hydraulic cylinder experiences when performing its sealing function. The sealing performance of the hydraulic cylinder in testing and operation must meet the specified conditions, among which the rated conditions are the design basis to ensure that the hydraulic cylinder has sufficient sealing life.

When designing the seal for a hydraulic cylinder, the first step is to determine the specified conditions. The allowable leakage of the hydraulic cylinder seal is also given under the specified conditions. The actual working conditions of the hydraulic cylinder are generally difficult to determine, that is, the specified conditions and actual conditions are different. This is because the extreme conditions of the hydraulic cylinder seal are
305:
( Extreme) operating conditions are difficult to predict, such as the instantaneous extreme velocity of piston and piston rod movement, sudden changes in hydraulic working medium and environmental temperature and conditions, sudden changes in external loads especially extreme side loads (eccentric loads) and pressure peak fluctuations, contamination caused by environmental changes, etc. These extreme operating conditions may occur for a very short time and be unrepeatable, but they can indeed cause hydraulic cylinder seal failure, and even develop into accidents.

Any sealing device or sealing system has the possibility of leakage and cannot adapt to all operating conditions, so it is very important to specify operating conditions in hydraulic cylinder seal design.

1. Specified operating conditions for hydraulic cylinder seals

Specified operating conditions are the operating conditions that the hydraulic cylinder must meet during operation or testing.

(1) Specified operating conditions in J B / T 1 0 2 0 5—2 0 1 0

J B / T 1 0 2 0 5—2 0 1 0 "Hydraulic Cylinder" is applicable to single and double-acting hydraulic cylinders with a nominal pressure below 31.5 MPa and hydraulic oil or other mineral oil with comparable performance as the working medium.

The basic parameters of the hydraulic cylinder include bore diameter, piston rod diameter, nominal pressure, stroke, installation dimensions, etc.

1) Pressure.

① The nominal pressure of the hydraulic cylinder should comply with the provisions of G B / T 2 3 4 6.

② The piston of the hydraulic cylinder is stopped at both ends of the stroke (single-acting hydraulic cylinder is at the extreme position of the stroke), and hydraulic oil with 1.5 times the nominal pressure is applied to the working chamber respectively. After a type test pressure retention of 2 min and a factory test pressure retention of 10 s, there should be no external leakage or component damage.

③ When the bore diameter of the hydraulic cylinder is greater than 32 mm, under the minimum pressure of 0.5 MPa; when the bore diameter of the hydraulic cylinder is less than or equal to 32 mm, under the pressure of 1 MPa, make the hydraulic cylinder reciprocate its full stroke more than 3 times, and stay at the end of the stroke for 10 s each time. During the test process, it should comply with:

a. The hydraulic cylinder should have no vibration or crawling.

b. There should be no hydraulic oil leakage at the piston rod seal. At the end of the test, the oil film on the piston rod should be insufficient to form oil droplets or oil rings.

c. There should be no hydraulic oil leakage at all static seals and welds.

d. There should be no hydraulic oil leakage in the throttling and (or) cushioning components installed on the hydraulic cylinder.

2) Kinematic viscosity of hydraulic oil. When the oil temperature is 40°C, the kinematic viscosity should be 29～74 mm²/s.

3) Working medium temperature.

① Generally, the working medium temperature of the hydraulic cylinder should be in the range of -20～80°C;

② Under the nominal pressure, input hydraulic oil at 90°C into the hydraulic cylinder, and reciprocate the full stroke for 1 h, which should comply with the agreement between the manufacturer and the user.

4) Ambient temperature. Generally, the working ambient temperature of the hydraulic cylinder should be in the range of -20～50°C.

5) Speed. Under the nominal pressure, the hydraulic cylinder runs continuously at the highest speed required by the design, with a speed error of ±10%, and runs continuously for more than 8 h each time. During the test, no adjustment shall be made to the components of the hydraulic cylinder, and the cumulative stroke or reversing times shall be recorded. After the test, all requirements shall comply with the durability requirements of the hydraulic cylinder.

2. Extreme Operating Conditions for Hydraulic Cylinder Seals

Extreme operating conditions refer to the maximum and/or minimum operating conditions that components, piping, or systems are allowed to operate under extreme conditions specified for a given application for a given time.

For example, the pressure test for hydraulic cylinders is: "Apply hydraulic oil at 1.5 times the nominal pressure to the working chambers respectively, and hold pressure for 10 s during factory testing, with no external leakage or component damage."

Since overpressure may also occur during pressure testing, generally overpressure ≤10%. To describe this situation, the operating conditions that occur instantaneously under extreme conditions are temporarily referred to as extreme conditions.

Extreme conditions should include:
1) Pressure peak: A pressure pulse that exceeds the corresponding steady-state pressure and even exceeds the maximum pressure.
2) Pressure intensification: Pressure intensification caused by piston area difference exceeding the rated pressure limit.
3) Gravity velocity: The extreme velocity at which free fall (gravity) acceleration gn=9.80665 m/s2 operates.
4) Ultra-low speed: When the inner diameter D of the hydraulic cylinder ≤200 mm, the lowest stable speed of the hydraulic cylinder is <4 mm/s; when the inner diameter D of the hydraulic cylinder >200 mm, the lowest stable speed of the hydraulic cylinder is <5 mm/s.
5) Excessive internal leakage during stroke: For hydraulic cylinders with a stroke exceeding 1 m, in addition to larger internal leakage at both ends of the stroke, the maximum internal leakage may occur at the middle position of the stroke.
6) Excessive leakage at low pressure: When the working pressure is lower than 0.5 MPa (or 1 MPa), the leakage at low pressure may exceed the standard.
7) Excessive operating temperature range: When the operating temperature is lower than -30°C or higher than 90°C.
8) Overload: In applications where overload or other external loads may be encountered, the design and installation of hydraulic cylinders should consider the maximum expected load or pressure peak.
9) Lateral or bending loads: Excessive deformation of the hydraulic cylinder structure due to structural design, installation, or alignment reasons.
10) Shock and vibration: Shock and vibration beyond the specified conditions of the hydraulic cylinder itself or its connecting parts.

3. Preliminary Determination of Rated Operating Conditions for Hydraulic Cylinder Seals

Rated operating conditions are the conditions indicated by the highest and lowest values (when necessary) of basic characteristics determined through testing. Components or piping are designed according to these conditions to ensure sufficient service life. However, in reality, some conditions, especially extreme conditions, are unrepeatable and therefore cannot be tested.

The design of hydraulic cylinder seals must provide specified conditions, but the specified conditions are a relatively ideal condition, and it is difficult to accurately provide them in actual design. Rated conditions can be gradually corrected based on testing, although some conditions, such as extreme conditions, cannot be tested. However, if the rated operating conditions for hydraulic cylinder seals are not specified, the hydraulic cylinder cannot be designed. Therefore, based on years of experience in hydraulic cylinder design practice, the author has referred to relevant standards, literature, and a large number of product samples from seal manufacturers, and has designed Table 2-157 for reference by hydraulic cylinder seal designers when determining the rated operating conditions for hydraulic cylinder seals.

(3) Comparison and Analysis of Load Efficiency
Load efficiency is not specified in GB/T24946-2010.
In GB/T13342-2007, JB/T10205-2010, and DB44/T11169.1-2013, the specified load efficiency requirements are that the load efficiency of hydraulic cylinders should not be less than 90%, the load efficiency of hydraulic cylinders should not be less than 90%, and the load efficiency of servo hydraulic cylinders should not be less than 90%, respectively.
In GB/T17446-2012, the general terminology related to efficiency is cylinder output force efficiency.
Static pressure support structures for piston rods are frequently used in electro-hydraulic servo valve controlled hydraulic cylinders. These structures incur certain hydraulic power losses whether using internal or external oil supply. Additionally, electro-hydraulic servo valve controlled hydraulic cylinders may have holes drilled in pistons to improve system stability, which also causes certain hydraulic power losses. Therefore, an indicator should be provided to reflect or calibrate the (total) efficiency of electro-hydraulic servo valve controlled hydraulic cylinders, providing a comprehensive evaluation of the utilization rate of input hydraulic power.
(4) Comparison and Analysis of External Leakage
External leakage is not specified in GB/T24946-2010, but sealing performance is specified, stating that when digital cylinders are subjected to 1.25 times the nominal pressure, there should be no external leakage at all mating surfaces.
JB/T10205-2010 specifies that piston rods (plunger rods) should not leak when stationary; DB44/T11169.1-2013 specifies that other parts should not leak when piston rods (plunger rods) are stationary; GB/T13342-2007 specifies that hydraulic cylinders should not leak externally at all seals and during movement.
For hydraulic cylinder piston rods, when the piston rod is moving, it is very difficult to achieve "zero" leakage. The so-called "zero" leakage condition theoretically occurs when the amount of hydraulic oil carried out by the rod equals the amount carried back, and this condition disappears immediately when conditions change.
Additionally, using "seepage" to describe the (external) leakage of hydraulic cylinder piston rods is not entirely appropriate. It is more suitable to express the leakage amount at the piston rod using Table 2-161.

(5) Comparison and Analysis of Durability
In GB/T 24946—2010, the durability specified for digital cylinders is that the service life under rated operating conditions should have a total accumulated stroke of not less than 105m.

The durability indicators specified in JB/T 10205—2010 and DB 44/T 11169.1—2013 are completely identical. In GB/T 13342—2007, the durability specified, except for single-acting piston cylinders or single-acting servo hydraulic cylinders, is the same as that specified in JB/T 10205—2010 and DB 44/T 11169.1—2013 for other types, but the durability requirements for plunger hydraulic cylinders are different, being "the external leakage of the hydraulic cylinder should not exceed 2 times the specified value."

The specification in GB/T 13342—2007 for the "external leakage" of plunger hydraulic cylinders after durability testing is more reasonable, because whether it is a single-acting plunger hydraulic cylinder or a single-acting servo hydraulic cylinder, there cannot be any internal leakage or increase in internal leakage after durability testing or before durability testing. Therefore, the requirement in JB/T 10205—2010 and DB 44/T 11169.1—2013 that "after durability testing, the increase in internal leakage should not exceed 2 times the specified value, and components should not have abnormal wear or other forms of damage" is not entirely reasonable.

GB/T 13342—2007 specifies the "external leakage" of plunger hydraulic cylinders after durability testing, which is also one of the reasons this manual references this standard. Otherwise, there would be no basis for determining the external leakage of plunger servo hydraulic cylinders after durability testing.

(6) Comparison and Analysis of Pressure Resistance
The pressure resistance requirement specified in GB/T 13342—2007 is that the hydraulic cylinder should withstand 1.5 times the nominal pressure without any component damage or permanent deformation, and without any leakage at gaskets and welds.

The pressure resistance requirements specified in GB/T 24946—2010 and DB 44/T 11169.1—2013 are basically the same, being that the digital cylinder should withstand 1.5 times the nominal pressure (pressure holding for 5 min), without any component damage or permanent deformation, without any leakage at welds, and the cylinder body of the servo hydraulic cylinder should withstand 1.5 times the nominal pressure, without any external leakage, component deformation, or damage during pressure holding for 5 min.

In JB/T 10205—2010, during pressure testing, the tested hydraulic cylinder piston should be stopped at both ends of the stroke (single-acting hydraulic cylinder at extreme position), and hydraulic fluid at 1.5 times the nominal pressure should be applied to the working chamber, with a pressure holding time of 2 min for type testing and 10 s for factory testing, without any external leakage or component damage.

Comparing the above four standards, the pressure resistance specified in JB/T 10205—2010 is more reasonable in terms of pressure holding time.

(7) Comparison and Analysis of Leakage at Low Pressure
GB/T 13342—2007 does not specify leakage at low pressure; GB/T 24946—2010 also does not specify leakage at low pressure.

The leakage at low pressure specified in JB/T 10205—2010 is: when the hydraulic cylinder bore is greater than 32mm, at the lowest pressure of 0.5MPa; when the hydraulic cylinder bore is less than or equal to 32mm, at a pressure of 1MPa, the hydraulic cylinder should reciprocate through its full stroke 3 or more times, with each end of the stroke held for at least 10s. During the test, it should meet the following...; b) no hydraulic fluid leakage at the piston rod seal, and at the end of the test, the oil film on the piston rod should not be sufficient to form oil drops or an oil ring; c) no hydraulic fluid leakage at all static seals and welds;...

The leakage at low pressure specified in DB 44/T 11169.1—2013 is: during testing of the servo hydraulic cylinder at a pressure of 3MPa, the oil cylinder should have no external leakage; at the end of the test, no oil drops or oil rings are allowed at the extended piston rod.

Comparing JB/T 10205—2010 and DB 44/T 11169.1—2013, the requirements for leakage at low pressure specified in these two standards are basically the same, but the description of hydraulic cylinder piston rod leakage in Table 2-161 is better.

Based on the above comparison and analysis, the main difference in the sealing technical requirements specified in DB 44/T 11169.1—2013 compared to those specified in other standards is in the "minimum starting pressure."

Further analysis of this main difference: Since servo hydraulic cylinders have dynamic performance requirements, their step response and frequency response both specify technical requirements (indicators). If the starting pressure is too high, the response speed will definitely be low. However, except for piston clearance seals, the minimum starting pressure indicators for combined seals specified in DB 44/T 11169.1—2013 are almost 1/10 or even lower than the indicators specified in current hydraulic cylinder standards, which raises questions about whether such a specification is reasonable from the perspective of servo hydraulic cylinder designers and manufacturers.

2. Selection of Seals for Servo Hydraulic Cylinders
Only referring to the products of a foreign seal manufacturer, based on the technical requirements for seals of servo (control) hydraulic cylinders, some piston combination seals are screened. However, if seals are selected according to the definition of "combination seal" in DB 44/T 11169.1—2013, it will be very difficult because the definition of combination seal given in this standard lacks the most basic connotation.

Still according to the definition of "combination seal" in GB/T 17446—2012, which is "a sealing device consisting of two or more units of different materials," seals are selected as shown in Table 2-162.

Sealing and friction are two aspects of the same issue and mutually restrict each other. If good sealing is required, the friction force may be large. Excessive pursuit of a low minimum starting pressure (which should be starting pressure, see GB/T 17446—2012) has little significance in hydraulic cylinder sealing, and this is also true for servo hydraulic cylinders, because the ratio of minimum starting pressure to nominal pressure is very small.

The minimum starting pressure indicator specified in DB 44/T 11169.1—2013 is too low, which is unscientific and unnecessary.

2.11 Design of Static Pressure Bearing Structure for Hydraulic Cylinder Piston Rod

1. General Provisions

The working principle of the piston rod static pressure bearing structure (liquid static pressure axial sliding bearing) is that the bearing force of the piston rod is mainly generated by the external fluid pressure, rather than by the relative motion (i.e., dynamic pressure effect) between the piston rod and its static pressure bearing sleeve.

The axial direction in the liquid static pressure axial sliding bearing refers to the relative motion form between the piston rod and its static pressure bearing sleeve, rather than the direction of the load it bears. The piston rod static pressure bearing structure in this manual includes sliding bearings and sliding bearing assemblies.

Generally, the design of the piston rod static pressure bearing structure should follow such a rule: under the maximum load that may be borne, the thickness of the lubrication clearance should be maintained at least 50% ~ 60% of the initial lubrication clearance.

When designing, the eccentricity (relative displacement amount after loading, ε = e / CR) should be limited to the range of ε = 0 ~ 0.5; in the calculation, it should be assumed that the throttling ratio ξ = 1, so that the static pressure bearing's stiffness characteristics are close to the optimal value.

It should also be considered that the load direction of the static pressure bearing structure, and it is necessary to distinguish between two extreme cases: the load acting on the center of the oil cavity and the load acting on the center of the sealing oil surface. In addition, special attention should be paid to a phenomenon caused by the bending deformation of the piston rod, which leads to misalignment of the shaft center, so that the piston rod contacts the edge of the static pressure bearing sleeve and damages the static pressure bearing structure.

The design and calculation of the piston rod static pressure bearing structure are based on a number of assumptions (including prerequisites and boundary conditions, etc.). Whether it is possible to accurately determine the functional relationship between its operating parameters and operating conditions, geometric shape, and hydraulic oil, i.e., many parameters such as eccentricity, bearing capacity, oil film stiffness, supply pressure, flow rate, friction power, temperature rise, etc., often require actual machine verification.

2. Structural Types

In common piston rod static pressure bearing structures, the static pressure bearing sleeve has a return oil groove between oil cavities, 4 or more even-numbered oil cavities, and the depth of the oil cavity is more than 10 times the lubricating clearance (radial clearance CR), and the length-to-diameter ratio B/D is 0.3 ~ 1, which is the most common structural type.

Compared with the structure without a return oil groove, this structure with a return oil groove requires greater supply power under the same stiffness.

The static pressure bearing sleeve and the cylinder head should have a reliable connection structure. If a medium-pressure interference fit is used, necessary measures should be taken to prevent the connection from being unreliable (unstable) or even failing under extreme conditions.

3. Basic Parameters

The basic parameters of the piston rod static pressure bearing structure include: inner diameter DB, outer diameter DO, width B of the static pressure bearing sleeve, number of oil cavities Z, axial sealing oil surface width la x, radial sealing oil surface width lc, return oil groove width bG, radial clearance (equivalent to bearing clearance) and type of throttle (such as orifice throttling type, capillary type, internal throttling type, etc.), size, etc.

4. Materials

Material of static pressure bearing sleeve (or bearing bush): Copper alloy should comply with the provisions of GB/T 18324-2001; cast copper alloy should comply with JB/T 7921-1995; forged copper alloy should comply with JB/T 7922-1995.

5. Geometric Dimensions, Geometric Tolerances

When designing, the axis of the inner hole of the static pressure bearing sleeve is generally determined as the datum element.

Only slight scratches are allowed on the outer circular surface, and they should not affect assembly and performance.

2.12 Design of Hydraulic Cylinder Buffer Device

Buffering is a means to decelerate when a moving part (such as a piston) approaches the end of its stroke. There are mainly two types: fixed (type) or adjustable (type), which are collectively classified as cylinders with buffers. The design of cylinders with fixed-type (hydraulic cylinder) buffer devices is one of the difficult points in hydraulic cylinder design.

For servo hydraulic cylinders, since soft limits can be set through the control system to avoid impact between moving parts and other cylinder parts, i.e., the working stroke range of the cylinder can be controlled, for some hydraulic cylinders with low movement speed, small moving part mass, or considering that even in special cases, collision will not cause external leakage of the cylinder and damage to cylinder parts, etc., it can be considered not to install a hydraulic cylinder buffer device.

The technical requirements for hydraulic cylinder buffer devices are generally derived from the technical conditions (requirements) of hydraulic machines (equipment), and should be adapted to the technical conditions (requirements) of the host machine. For example, in JB/T38182014 "Technical Conditions for Hydraulic Presses", the following specific provisions are made for hydraulic cylinders for hydraulic presses: hydraulic driving elements (such as pistons, columns, sliders, moving worktables, etc.) should not have vibration, crawling, and stagnation phenomena within the specified stroke and speed range, and should not have impact phenomena that affect normal operation during commutation and pressure relief.

2.12.1 Technical Requirements for Fixed-Type Buffer Devices for Hydraulic Cylinders

1. Technical requirements for fixed-type buffer devices specified in various standards

For cylinders with fixed-type buffer devices, their buffering performance cannot be adjusted online, and this does not include the situation where the buffering performance is changed by changing the viscosity of the working medium (hydraulic oil).

In the product standards for hydraulic cylinders, there are two standards that put forward technical requirements for fixed-type hydraulic cylinder buffer devices:

1) In CB/T38122013 "Hydraulic Cylinder for Hatch Cover of Ships", it is stipulated that under the condition that the test hydraulic cylinder is input with a pressure of 50% of the nominal pressure, and tested at the designed highest speed, the buffering effect is that the piston should be smooth and slow when entering the buffer area.

2) In QC/T46020101 "Technical Conditions for Hydraulic Cylinders for Dump Trucks", it is stipulated that when the hydraulic cylinder is fully extended, the piston rod should extend and retract at a speed of 50~70mm/s, and there should be no impact sound when the hydraulic cylinder automatically stops.

2. General technical requirements for buffer devices

In addition to the above-mentioned performance requirements for fixed-type hydraulic cylinder buffer devices specified in the standards, the following basic performance requirements should be met as much as possible when designing fixed-type hydraulic cylinder buffer devices:

1) The buffer device should be able to absorb the maximum kinetic energy with a shorter buffer length of the cylinder (also called buffer stroke), that is, the kinetic energy of the moving parts (including various connecting parts or related parts) should be completely converted into thermal energy.

2) During the buffering process, pressure pulsation and excessively high peak pressure in the buffer cavity should be avoided as much as possible, so that the change in pressure is a gradual process.

3) The peak buffering pressure in the buffer cavity (rodless end) should be less than or equal to 1.5 times the nominal pressure of the hydraulic cylinder.
324:
4) When a buffer device is installed at the rodless end, the buffer pressure should avoid acting on the dynamic seal system of the piston rod.

5) The conversion of kinetic energy into thermal energy causes the hydraulic oil temperature to rise, and the maximum oil temperature should not exceed the maximum allowable operating temperature of the seal.

6) According to JB/T 10205-2010 "Hydraulic Cylinder", when the hydraulic cylinder has requirements for buffer performance, it should be determined through negotiation between the user and the manufacturer.

7) The starting performance of the hydraulic cylinder should be considered, and the minimum starting pressure of the hydraulic cylinder should not exceed the provisions of relevant standards; Abnormal situations such as delayed movement or abnormal movement, and abnormal noise should be avoided when the piston starts or leaves the buffer zone.

3. Ideal Buffer Performance Expected in Buffer Device Design

1) Adapt to working condition changes and can be adjusted within a certain range, such as changes in hydraulic oil viscosity, ambient temperature changes, changes in the speed of the piston at the beginning of buffering, changes in the return pressure of the hydraulic cylinder, changes in the gravity of related moving parts, etc.

2) During the buffering process, maintain a constant buffer pressure, and the deceleration of the piston is constant.

3) During buffering, the temperature rise of the hydraulic oil should not exceed 55°C, and the maximum temperature should not exceed 80°C.

4) If there is a pressure peak in the buffer cavity, it should not be greater than 1.5 times the nominal pressure of the hydraulic cylinder.

5) When the piston reaches the end of the cylinder return stroke, its moving speed should be zero, and there should be no abnormal noise or rebound.

6) There should be no abnormal noise or abnormal movement when the cylinder process starts, that is, there should be no excessive buffering problem.

7) The structure should be simple, easy to adjust, low manufacturing cost, and facilitate mass processing and manufacturing.

4. Design Principles of Hydraulic Cylinder Buffer Device

1) When the moving speed of the hydraulic cylinder piston is ≤100 mm/s, it can be considered not to install a buffer device; When the moving speed of the piston is >200 mm/s, a buffer device must be installed.

2) For double-acting hydraulic cylinders without a variable throttle buffer device at the rodless end, the most ideal buffer plunger is a concave parabolic shape. Therefore, efforts should be made to design and process the buffer plunger to be close to a concave parabolic shape (mainly using a conical or double-conical shape).

3) The end of the buffer plunger should not hit the cylinder bottom, and the buffer device should be protected during structural design.

4) The speed after buffering and restarting should not be too fast, and the buffer side (rodless end) should not be subjected to cavitation.

5) When a buffer device is installed at the rodless end, the buffer pressure should avoid acting on the dynamic seal system of the piston rod.

6) Comply with the general technical requirements for hydraulic cylinder buffer device design.

5. Basis for Hydraulic Cylinder Buffer Device Design

1) Moving speed of moving parts. If the cylinder is fixed and the piston rod is in the return stroke, the return speed of the piston rod is the basis for design.

2) Mass of moving parts. If the cylinder is fixed and the piston rod is in the return stroke, the mass of the piston rod is the basis for design; If the piston rod is connected to a slider, the mass of the slider should also be considered; If two (or more) cylinders control one slider, the mass conversion should also be included.

3) Load (gravity) and the direction of motion speed, such as whether it is an overload.

4) The (control) pressure and flow rate of the other cavity of the hydraulic cylinder during buffering.

5) Control method for buffering stop (end).

6) The situation (requirements) of restarting after buffering should not only consider the buffering effect but also the starting effect.

7) Temperature change range of hydraulic oil.

8) Expected design life of the buffer device.

3) The calculation formula for the annular throttling gap (single side) \(\delta\) can only be used for approximate calculation, not only for the above reasons, but also because the reason for the formation of the gap flow is not only the pressure difference flow caused by the pressure difference, but also the shear flow caused by the movement of the buffer plunger.

4) The gap (annular throttling gap) \(\delta\) between the buffer plunger and the buffer hole (single side) should not be designed too small. According to the size and tolerance of the hydraulic cylinder and its parts and the requirements of geometric accuracy, it is generally taken as \(\delta \geq 0.10 \sim 0.12 \, \text{mm}\). If \(\delta\) is designed and selected too small, it may also cause collision or rubbing between the buffer plunger and the cylinder head (the buffer hole set on the bottom of the cylinder) due to reasons such as the assembly of the hydraulic cylinder assembly, the processing quality of each component, and the wear of the guide sleeve (ring) that may cause eccentricity.

2.12.2 Buffer Device with Adjustable Buffer Valve
The buffer device with adjustable buffer valve consists of a buffer valve and a throttle valve. The buffer valve is typically installed on the piston, and the throttle valve is installed on the piston rod. The buffer valve can be a throttle valve or a throttle hole, and the throttle valve can be a throttle valve, a throttle hole (for cylindrical holes), or a buffer device with non-cylindrical throttle holes.
During the buffering process, the ideal buffer device should maintain a constant buffer pressure, and the piston acceleration should be constant. According to the above assumptions, the piston acceleration a (m/s²) is
a = am = v₀² / (2sc) (2-71)
Then the buffer pressure pc (MPa) is
pc = pcm = [A₁p₁sc + (1 - 2×G/(gv₀²±Rsc))]×10⁻⁶ / Asc (2-72)
Then the buffer time tc (s) is
tc = 2sc / vo (s) (2-73)
The throttling area Ai (m²) relative to the buffer stroke s is
Ai = Aρv₀ / (Cd²gΔp×10⁻⁶) / vi (2-74)
or
Ai = Aρv₀ / (Cd²Δp×10⁻⁶) / vi (2-75)
The above formula for the throttling area relative to the buffer stroke s is derived from the thin-wall orifice flow formula Q = CdA₀√(2Δp/ρ). During the buffering process, the piston velocity vi at time t (i.e., ti) should be (under the condition that the piston acceleration is constant, i.e., uniform deceleration a = am = -v₀²/(2sc)) vi = v₀ - (v₀²/(2sc))ti; under the same conditions, the piston stroke s at time t (i.e., ti) should be s = v₀t - (v₀²/(4sc))t²i. From the above two equations and the boundary condition t ≤ tc (buffer time tc = 2sc/v₀), we can obtain
vi = v₀√(sc-s)/√(sc) (2-76)
Then the above calculation formula for the throttling area Ai relative to the buffer stroke s is
Ai = A√(ρv₀/(Cd²Δp×10⁻⁶)) × √(sc-s)/√(sc) (2-77)
This formula is the variable throttling instantaneous throttling area calculation formula, which is the basis for designing the buffer plunger shape.
However, the actual throttling orifice is not a thin-wall orifice, and the flow coefficient Cd is not a constant, and it is difficult to set (test) accurately, so there is a gap between the calculated results and the test results, which must be corrected through testing. If the above formula is derived according to the long-hole throttling formula, the same problem exists.
2.12.3 Technical Requirements for Buffer Devices with Buffer Valves in Hydraulic Cylinders
For hydraulic cylinders with adjustable buffer devices, their buffer performance can be adjusted online, and the buffer valve buffer device is such a buffer device, but the buffer valve (group) here is different from the buffer valve usually used in hydraulic systems.
In the product standards for hydraulic cylinders, the following three standards have proposed technical (test) requirements for buffer valve hydraulic cylinder buffer devices:
1) In GB/T15622-2005 "Test Method for Hydraulic Cylinders", it is stipulated that all buffer valves in the working chamber of the tested cylinder should be fully loosened, the test pressure should be adjusted to 50% of the nominal pressure, and the cylinder should be moved at the designed maximum speed to detect the buffer effect when the buffer valve is fully closed.
2) In JB/T10205-2010 "Hydraulic Cylinder", it is stipulated that all buffer valves in the working chamber of the tested cylinder should be fully loosened, the test pressure should be adjusted to 50% of the nominal pressure, and the cylinder should be moved at the designed maximum speed. When the buffer valve is fully closed, the buffer effect should meet the requirements of 6.2.8, i.e., the buffer performance requirements for hydraulic cylinders should be determined by negotiation between the user and the manufacturer. At the same time, it is required that the installed throttling and (or) buffer components (should) have no hydraulic oil leakage.
3) In JB/T11588-2013 "Large Hydraulic Cylinders", it is stipulated that all buffer valves in the working chamber of the tested cylinder should be fully loosened, the test pressure should be adjusted to 50% of the nominal pressure, and the cylinder should be moved at the designed maximum speed to detect the buffer effect when the buffer valve is fully closed.
Author's note: In JB/T11588-2013, there are no requirements for buffer effect or performance.
Although GB/T15622-2005 is not quoted in the normative references of JB/T11588-2013, the content of technical requirements for buffering in the above three standards is almost the same.
Regardless of whether the installed buffer device is a fixed or adjustable type, it should comply with the requirements of JB/T10205-2010, i.e., the installed throttling and (or) buffer components have no hydraulic oil (external) leakage.

2.1.3.5 Technical requirements for speed sensors for hydraulic cylinders

A speed sensor is a sensor that can sense speed and convert it into a usable output signal. Technical requirements for speed sensors are specified in GB/T30242-2013.
